strategies.name: Moving Average Crossover
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses a faster and a slower moving average. When the fast line crosses the slow line, the trend is treated as changing.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how traders use two moving averages to define trend direction and spot potential trend changes.
strategies.core_concept: Prices tend to persist in trends (momentum). Averaging smooths out noise, so a crossover marks a shift in average price direction. It reacts after a move starts, not before.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: SMA or EMA. Common pairs are 50/200 daily ("golden cross"/"death cross"), 20/50, 9/21 (intraday) and 10/30.

rules.entry: Go long when the fast MA closes above the slow MA, or short on the reverse.
rules.exit: Exit on the opposite crossover. A variant exits when price closes beyond the slow MA.
rules.stop: Below the recent swing low, or an ATR multiple (e.g. 2–3× ATR(14)).

asset_class_notes.forex: Major pairs have long trend phases but also long ranges. Swap and spread costs matter on frequent signals.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Indices are often used as a regime filter (above or below the 200-day). Individual stocks are prone to gaps.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Strong trends suit it, but extreme volatility and 24/7 trading produce many whipsaws on low timeframes.
asset_class_notes.futures: This is the classic home of trend systems. Handle contract rolls carefully in backtests.

market_conditions.struggles: Sideways markets, where repeated crossovers cause whipsaws.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Lag: entries come late and exits give back open profit.

common_pitfalls: Optimising MA lengths to past data (curve fitting).
Trading every crossover in a range.
Treating the golden cross as a standalone "buy signal" headline.
strategies.win_rate_note: Educators sometimes imply crossovers catch every trend. In practice, trend-following systems typically have fewer than half their trades turn a profit — a minority of large winners pays for many small losses. That's normal for this design, not a sign it's failing. A claim that this specific setup wins most of the time is a red flag.

evidence.summary: Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (1992) found strong support on DJIA data from 1897 to 1986. Later data-snooping and out-of-sample tests found the edge failed after the sample period (Sullivan, Timmermann and White 1999) or disappeared after low transaction costs (Bajgrowicz and Scaillet 2012). Diversified multi-market trend following has stronger support (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012).

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView ("MA Cross"). Easy to code in Pine Script.
sources: StockCharts ChartSchool, "Moving Averages – Simple and Exponential"
Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992), Journal of Finance 47(5)
Sullivan, Timmermann & White (1999), Journal of Finance 54(5)

step_by_step.title: Pick your two moving averages
step_by_step.detail: Choose a faster (shorter-period) and slower (longer-period) moving average. Classic combinations: 50/200-day for long-term "golden cross"/"death cross" signals, 20/50 for swing trading, or 9/21 EMA for faster intraday signals. EMAs react quicker to recent price than SMAs, which is why most short-term traders prefer them.

step_by_step.title: Add both to your chart
step_by_step.detail: On TradingView (or any charting platform), open Indicators, search "Moving Average" (or "EMA" for exponential), add it twice with your two chosen periods, and give them different colours so you can tell them apart at a glance.

step_by_step.title: Wait for the actual crossover, not just a close line
step_by_step.detail: A valid signal is the faster line crossing fully above (bullish) or below (bearish) the slower line, ideally confirmed by a candle close — not just a brief intrabar touch that reverses a moment later.

step_by_step.title: Check if other evidence agrees before entering
step_by_step.detail: Don't trade the crossover blind. Look at whether price is also above a longer-term trend filter (like a 200-day MA), whether volume is picking up, and whether an oscillator like RSI isn't already extremely stretched in the opposite direction.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the next candle's open after confirmation
step_by_step.detail: Many traders wait for the crossover candle to fully close, then enter at the next candle's open — this avoids reacting to a crossover that reverses intrabar before the candle finishes.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop before you place your trade
step_by_step.detail: Put your stop-loss below the most recent swing low (for a long) or above the most recent swing high (for a short) — decide this before you're in the position, not after.

step_by_step.title: Decide your exit rule in advance
step_by_step.detail: Common choices: exit on the opposite crossover, exit when price closes back through the slower MA, or use a trailing stop that follows price up. Pick one before you enter, not while you're already holding and emotional.

strategies.name: Support and Resistance Trading
strategies.summary_one_line: Treats price areas where the market previously turned as zones where it may react again.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how traders mark price zones where buying or selling previously appeared and how those zones are used to plan trades.
strategies.core_concept: Market memory and clustering of orders. Many participants anchor to prior highs and lows and to round numbers, so orders cluster there. A broken level often switches roles (support becomes resistance, and the reverse).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Horizontal lines or zones at swing highs and lows, prior day/week highs and lows, and round numbers. Treat them as zones, not exact lines.

rules.entry: Bounce: buy near support or sell near resistance after a rejection signal. Break-and-retest: enter after a close through the level and a retest.
rules.exit: Target the next opposing level.

asset_class_notes.forex: Round numbers (e.g. 1.1000) are widely watched. Levels around session opens (London/New York) matter.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Prior highs/lows, gaps and earnings levels.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Psychological round numbers are very prominent. Expect frequent stop runs.

market_conditions.works_best: Bounce trades suit ranges, and break trades suit expansion.
market_conditions.struggles: Choppy conditions around an obvious level.
market_conditions.failure_modes: False breakouts and "stop hunts" through obvious levels.

common_pitfalls: Hindsight-drawn levels that look perfect on past charts.
Placing stops exactly at obvious levels.
strategies.win_rate_note: Courses often present "sniper" level entries with tight stops and imply a high proportion of winners. Outcomes depend heavily on how levels and confirmation are defined. Bounce trades can have a moderate-to-high proportion of winners with modest reward-to-risk; break trades usually have fewer winners but bigger ones.

evidence.summary: Little direct testing, because levels are subjective. Osler's Federal Reserve Bank of New York research on intraday FX found that published support/resistance levels had some ability to predict trend interruptions — narrow, older evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual drawing tools on TradingView. Pivot-based auto-levels exist in community scripts.

image.caption: Synthetic price action bouncing between a marked support and resistance zone.

step_by_step.title: Strip your chart back to candles only
step_by_step.detail: Remove every indicator first. Support and resistance come from where price itself has repeatedly reacted — overlaying indicators at this stage just adds noise.

step_by_step.title: Pick the right lookback for your timeframe
step_by_step.detail: For swing or position trading, use the daily chart with 12–18 months of history. For day trading, use a 15-minute chart with roughly 3–6 months.

step_by_step.title: Mark swing highs and lows
step_by_step.detail: Find the peaks and troughs where price clearly changed direction — not every minor wiggle in between.

step_by_step.title: Only keep levels price has reacted at 2–3+ times
step_by_step.detail: A level only matters if price has stalled, reversed, or paused there more than once. One touch isn't a level, it's a coincidence.

step_by_step.title: Draw a zone, not a single line
step_by_step.detail: Real markets rarely reverse at one exact price. Draw a band a few points or pips wide around the cluster of reactions instead of a single precise line.

step_by_step.title: Wait for price to return, then wait again for a reaction candle
step_by_step.detail: Don't buy the moment price touches support. Wait for a rejection candle (a hammer, pin bar, or bullish engulfing at support) that confirms buyers actually showed up there.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop just beyond the zone, target the next level
step_by_step.detail: Stop-loss goes just past the zone, not right at its exact edge (which gets hunted often). Target the next clear support/resistance level in the direction of your trade.

step_by_step.title: Remember broken levels can flip roles
step_by_step.detail: Once resistance is convincingly broken — a strong close through it, ideally with volume — it often becomes support on the next pullback, and the same works in reverse.

strategies.name: Trendline Trading
strategies.summary_one_line: Draws a line along rising lows (uptrend) or falling highs (downtrend); traders buy pullbacks to the line or watch for a break.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how trendlines are drawn and how traders use them to frame pullbacks and trend breaks.
strategies.core_concept: In trends, pullbacks often stop at similar slopes. A break of the line suggests that momentum is changing.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: A line through at least two swing points, with a third touch treated as confirmation. Channels add a parallel line.

rules.entry: A touch plus rejection in the trend direction.
rules.exit: A decisive close through the line is treated as a possible exit or reversal setup.
rules.stop: Beyond the line or the last swing.

asset_class_notes.stocks: On log versus linear charts, lines differ meaningfully for assets with big percentage moves.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Often violates lines intrabar given high volatility.
asset_class_notes.futures: Usable; watch contract rolls on continuous charts.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy trends, where steep lines break easily.
market_conditions.failure_modes: A "break" that resumes the trend rather than reversing it.

strategies.win_rate_note: "Three-touch" claims of reliability are common in marketing. Real results vary with the drawing rules — there's no standard profile because the method isn't standardised.

evidence.summary: Very little rigorous testing because of subjectivity. Automated pattern studies (Lo, Mamaysky and Wang 2000) treat related geometry but not trendlines directly.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual drawing on TradingView. Auto-trendline community scripts exist but differ in definitions.
sources: Edwards & Magee, "Technical Analysis of Stock Trends"

image.caption: A trendline drawn through a series of fabricated swing lows.

step_by_step.title: Confirm you're actually in a trend first
step_by_step.detail: Trendlines only work when there's a real trend — a clear sequence of higher highs and higher lows (up) or lower highs and lower lows (down). Forcing a trendline onto a sideways market gives you nonsense.

step_by_step.title: Find at least two swing points to anchor the line
step_by_step.detail: For an uptrend, find two (ideally three) rising swing LOWS. For a downtrend, find two to three falling swing HIGHS. A very common beginner mistake is connecting the highs in an uptrend instead of the lows — don't do that.

step_by_step.title: Draw the line through those points, not through the candles
step_by_step.detail: The line should touch the wicks (or bodies — see the next step) at the swing points without slicing through price action elsewhere on the chart.

step_by_step.title: Be consistent with wicks vs. bodies
step_by_step.detail: Pick one method — always use wicks, or always use candle bodies — and stick with it for that line. Don't mix them partway through.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a third touch before trusting the line
step_by_step.detail: Two points define a line mathematically, but the market hasn't "confirmed" it's respecting that line until price touches it a third time and reacts.

step_by_step.title: Trade the bounce, or trade the break
step_by_step.detail: Bounce: enter in the trend direction when price touches the line and shows a rejection candle, with your stop just beyond the line. Break: a decisive close through the line can signal the trend is changing — many traders wait for a retest of the broken line before entering.

step_by_step.title: Re-draw as new swings form
step_by_step.detail: A trendline isn't permanent. As the trend progresses and makes new swing points, you'll often need to redraw a steeper or shallower line to match the new structure.

strategies.name: RSI Overbought/Oversold
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses the Relative Strength Index to flag stretched conditions: above 70 is "overbought" and below 30 is "oversold".
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how the RSI oscillator measures recent momentum and how traders interpret its overbought and oversold zones.
strategies.core_concept: Short-term price extremes sometimes partially reverse. RSI compares the size of recent gains to recent losses on a 0–100 scale (J. Welles Wilder, 1978).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: RSI(14), with levels at 70/30. Variants use 80/20 or a 50 midline for trend.

rules.entry: Buy when RSI crosses back above 30, or sell when it crosses back below 70. A trend-aware variant only takes oversold buys in uptrends (e.g. price above the 200-day MA).
rules.exit: At the midline (50) or the opposite zone.

asset_class_notes.forex: Ranges during the Asian session suit reversion. Avoid fading around major news.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Index ETFs have historically shown more short-term reversion than strongly trending single stocks.
asset_class_notes.crypto: RSI can stay "overbought" for long periods in strong trends.
asset_class_notes.futures: Equity index futures are used similarly to indices.

market_conditions.struggles: Strong trends — overbought can stay overbought.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Selling strength into a powerful rally gives repeated losses.

strategies.win_rate_note: Mean-reversion rules often show a high proportion of winning trades with small average gains and occasional large losses, especially without stops. Marketing that headlines how often it wins hides that tail — treat any "high-accuracy RSI" claim with caution.

evidence.summary: A 2016 International Review of Financial Analysis study of 22 currencies found some RSI-based rules remained robust after data-snooping control in 2006–2015, while traditional rules did not. In equities, broad reviews show weak results after costs.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView. Easy in Pine Script.
sources: Wilder, "New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems" (1978)

image.caption: Synthetic price with a 14-period RSI panel showing the 70/30 overbought/oversold zones.

step_by_step.title: Add RSI to your chart
step_by_step.detail: On TradingView: Indicators > Relative Strength Index. The default period is 14 — leave it there unless you have a specific, tested reason to change it.

step_by_step.title: Draw your reference lines at 70 and 30
step_by_step.detail: These are usually already there by default: 70 = overbought, 30 = oversold. Some traders use 80/20 instead, which reduces false signals but also reduces how often you get a signal at all.

step_by_step.title: Identify the broader trend first
step_by_step.detail: Check whether price is above or below a longer moving average (like the 200-period). This matters because the standard overbought/oversold levels behave very differently depending on that backdrop.

step_by_step.title: In a genuine range: trade both directions
step_by_step.detail: If price is truly range-bound (not trending), look for longs when RSI dips below 30 and turns back up, and shorts when it pokes above 70 and turns back down.

step_by_step.title: In a trend: only take signals in the trend's direction
step_by_step.detail: If price is in a clear uptrend, treat RSI dips to 30–40 as potential buy zones and largely ignore overbought readings — in a strong uptrend, RSI can sit above 70 for a long stretch without the trend reversing. Mirror this logic for downtrends.

step_by_step.title: Wait for RSI to actually turn, not just touch the level
step_by_step.detail: Don't enter the instant RSI touches 30 or 70. Wait for it to cross back through that level, confirming momentum is genuinely shifting rather than just brushing the level and continuing on.

step_by_step.title: Plan your stop and exit together
step_by_step.detail: Set a stop beyond the recent price swing. A common exit rule is closing the trade when RSI reaches the 50 midline, or when it reaches the opposite extreme.

strategies.name: MACD Signal-Line Crossover
strategies.summary_one_line: Watches the MACD line cross its signal line as a shift in short-term momentum.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how the MACD indicator tracks momentum and what a signal-line crossover is meant to show.
strategies.core_concept: MACD is the difference between two EMAs, and the signal line is an EMA of MACD (Gerald Appel). Crossovers mark acceleration or deceleration of the trend.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: MACD(12, 26, 9), with a histogram showing MACD minus signal.

rules.entry: Long when MACD crosses above the signal line (often only above zero, in trend), with the reverse for shorts.
rules.exit: On the opposite crossover.
rules.stop: At the swing low/high or an ATR multiple.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Weekly MACD is used for stock index regime.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Fast moves make crossovers very frequent on low timeframes.

market_conditions.struggles: Ranges, which produce whipsaws.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Lag in sharp reversals.

common_pitfalls: Stacking MACD with other EMA-based tools (they're redundant).
strategies.win_rate_note: Similar profile to MA crossovers: a moderate-to-low proportion of trades win, relying on occasional larger trend gains. Treat "high-accuracy MACD" claims as marketing.

evidence.summary: MACD is a variant of MA rules, so the MA literature applies: historical support that fades after snooping and cost adjustments.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.
sources: Appel, "Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors"

image.caption: Synthetic price with an oscillator panel illustrating a momentum signal crossing its trigger line.

step_by_step.title: Add MACD with the standard settings
step_by_step.detail: 12, 26, 9 is the default almost everyone uses — don't change these unless you have a specific, tested reason to.

step_by_step.title: Learn to read all three parts
step_by_step.detail: The MACD line (faster EMA minus slower EMA), the signal line (an EMA of the MACD line), and the histogram (the gap between them). Most beginners only watch the two lines and ignore the histogram, which actually gives the earliest hint of a shift.

step_by_step.title: Check which side of the zero line you're on
step_by_step.detail: MACD above zero means the faster average is above the slower one — a long-bias backdrop. Below zero means a short-bias backdrop. Crossovers happening near or just after crossing zero tend to catch the start of new momentum; crossovers deep into overbought or oversold territory are often late.

step_by_step.title: Wait for the actual crossover
step_by_step.detail: A buy signal is the MACD line crossing above the signal line; a sell signal is it crossing below.

step_by_step.title: Don't jump in on the crossover candle itself
step_by_step.detail: Wait for that candle to close, then enter on the next candle's open. This small delay filters out a lot of signals that would have reversed intrabar.

step_by_step.title: Check for confluence before pulling the trigger
step_by_step.detail: Is price also above or below a key moving average? Is RSI not already extremely stretched the other way? Is volume reasonable? MACD alone throws off a lot of false signals in a quiet, range-bound market.

step_by_step.title: Plan your stop and exit before entering
step_by_step.detail: Stop below the recent swing low (long) or above the recent swing high (short). A common exit rule is simply the opposite crossover, though some traders exit earlier when the histogram starts shrinking — momentum fading — rather than waiting for the full reverse cross.

strategies.name: Bollinger Band Basics
strategies.summary_one_line: Plots bands two standard deviations around a 20-period average; traders use band touches for reversion and band expansions for breakouts.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how Bollinger Bands adapt to volatility and the two main ways traders read them.
strategies.core_concept: Volatility clusters, and prices far from their average relative to recent volatility are "stretched". John Bollinger stresses that a band touch alone is not a signal.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: BB(20, 2), plus optional %B and Bandwidth.

rules.entry: Reversion: in a range, buy a close back inside the lower band. Breakout ("band walk"): after a narrowing ("squeeze"), trade a close outside the band in the direction of the break.
rules.exit: Reversion targets the middle band.
rules.stop: Below the extreme (reversion) or inside the squeeze (breakout).

asset_class_notes.stocks: Index futures are used for intraday reversion.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Often "walks the band" in trends, which punishes fading.
asset_class_notes.futures: Used for intraday reversion on index futures.

market_conditions.works_best: Reversion suits ranges; breakout suits volatility expansion.
market_conditions.struggles: Fading a trend that walks the band.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Treating the upper band as an automatic "sell".

common_pitfalls: Mixing up the two opposite uses.
strategies.win_rate_note: Reversion variants tend to win more often with occasional large losses; breakout variants win less often with larger winners. Marketing often quotes only the reversion figure.

evidence.summary: The 2016 FX study found Bollinger-based rules robustly profitable across currencies in its recent sub-sample, a rare positive post-2006 result. Equity evidence is thin.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

image.caption: Fabricated price action with Bollinger Bands expanding and contracting around a moving average.

step_by_step.title: Add Bollinger Bands with the default settings
step_by_step.detail: A 20-period moving average with 2 standard deviations is John Bollinger's own recommended default, and what nearly every tutorial assumes you're using.

step_by_step.title: Figure out which of the two opposite strategies fits right now
step_by_step.detail: Bollinger Bands are used in two contradictory ways depending on conditions: fading touches of the bands in a RANGE, or riding a "band walk" breakout when volatility expands. Using the wrong one for current conditions is the single biggest beginner mistake with this tool.

step_by_step.title: For range/reversion trading: wait for a touch plus a reaction
step_by_step.detail: In a sideways market with a flat middle band, a touch of the lower band plus a bullish reversal candle is a buy signal, targeting the middle band first and then the opposite band. Mirror this at the upper band for shorts.

step_by_step.title: For breakout trading: watch for "the squeeze"
step_by_step.detail: When the bands pinch tightly together (low volatility), that's often the calm before a bigger move. Wait for a candle to close clearly outside the bands, ideally with volume well above average, and trade in that breakout direction.

step_by_step.title: Never fade a band walk
step_by_step.detail: If price is "walking the band" — repeatedly touching or hugging the upper or lower band during a strong trend — don't fight it by fading every touch. That's the classic way this strategy loses money.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop based on which variant you're trading
step_by_step.detail: Reversion trades: stop just beyond the band you faded. Breakout trades: stop back inside the squeeze range.

step_by_step.title: Use band width as a standalone volatility gauge too
step_by_step.detail: Even without taking a trade, watching the bands narrow and widen tells you whether the market is calm or active right now — useful context for every other strategy you run alongside this one.

strategies.name: Simple Range Breakout
strategies.summary_one_line: Marks a recent high/low range and trades in the direction price escapes it.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how traders define a price range and plan around a move out of it.
strategies.core_concept: Consolidations store orders. A break may trigger stops and new positioning, which can start a trend. Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron tested a "trading range break" rule.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: The recent N-bar high/low (e.g. 20 bars), or a visually defined box. ATR is used for stops.

rules.entry: On a close (or a trade) beyond the range.
rules.exit: A trailing stop, or a measured move (range height projected).
rules.stop: Back inside the range or at the opposite side.

asset_class_notes.forex: London-open breakouts of the Asian range are a popular variant.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Breakouts on rising volume are preferred.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Frequent fake-outs around weekends and low liquidity.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy, range-bound conditions.
market_conditions.failure_modes: False breakouts that reverse back into the range.

common_pitfalls: Placing stops too tight inside noise.
strategies.win_rate_note: Breakout systems typically have fewer winning trades than losing ones, with gains coming from the minority of breakouts that run.

evidence.summary: Trading-range-break rules were supported in BLL (1992) on historical DJIA data. Later data-snooping-robust work (Sullivan, Timmermann and White 1999; Bajgrowicz and Scaillet 2012) undermines their out-of-sample value in mature equity indices. Breakouts are a core component of trend-following systems with stronger diversified evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Easy in Pine Script; Donchian Channels are built in.

image.caption: Synthetic price consolidating in a range before breaking out to the upside.

step_by_step.title: Define your range
step_by_step.detail: Most commonly the first 5–30 minutes of a session (an "opening range"), but the same logic works on any clearly-bounded consolidation — mark the highest high and lowest low of that period.

step_by_step.title: Draw the range boundaries on your chart
step_by_step.detail: A horizontal line at the range high and another at the range low. This is now your reference for the rest of the session or move.

step_by_step.title: Don't jump the gun on a wick
step_by_step.detail: Wait for an actual candle CLOSE beyond the range boundary, not just a brief poke through it, before treating it as a real breakout.

step_by_step.title: Check volume on the breakout candle
step_by_step.detail: A breakout on volume clearly above the recent average is far more trustworthy than one on thin volume — low-volume breakouts fail ("fake out") much more often.

step_by_step.title: Enter at the break, or wait for a retest
step_by_step.detail: Aggressive approach: enter as soon as the breakout candle closes. More conservative approach: wait for price to pull back and retest the broken level as support/resistance before entering — a tighter stop, at the cost of sometimes missing the move entirely.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop back inside the range
step_by_step.detail: For a long breakout, stop just below the range high (which should now act as support), or below the range low for a wider stop. Mirror this above the range low for a short.

step_by_step.title: Use a fixed reward-to-risk target, like 2:1
step_by_step.detail: A common, simple rule: whatever you're risking to your stop, target twice that in profit — though many traders instead trail their stop once the move is working, to let bigger trends run further.

videos.note: A concise, specific walkthrough of the opening-range version of this strategy, the most common way it's actually traded.

strategies.name: Candlestick Reversal Basics (Engulfing, Pin Bar/Hammer)
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses specific one- to three-candle shapes as possible signs of a turn, especially at key levels.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how to read engulfing candles and pin bars and why context matters more than the pattern itself.
strategies.core_concept: Candles summarise the battle between buyers and sellers within a bar. A long rejection wick or an engulfing body suggests the other side has taken control. This comes from Japanese rice trading and was popularised in the West by Steve Nison.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Candlestick chart only. Optional filters are trend, support/resistance, and volume.

rules.entry: At support, a bullish engulfing or hammer prompts a long above the pattern high (mirror at resistance for shorts).
rules.exit: The next level or a fixed R multiple.
rules.stop: Below the pattern low (or above the high for shorts).

asset_class_notes.forex: Many brokers' daily candle closes differ by time zone, which changes the patterns — use a consistent New York-close feed.
asset_class_notes.crypto: The 24/7 market means the "daily close" is arbitrary.

market_conditions.works_best: At meaningful levels after an extended move.
market_conditions.struggles: Isolated patterns in the middle of a range, which are noise.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Pattern-spotting everywhere regardless of context.

common_pitfalls: Memorising dozens of named patterns without testing.
strategies.win_rate_note: Pattern-encyclopedia marketing often quotes high reliability percentages for these shapes. Rigorous tests do not support that confidence.

evidence.summary: Marshall, Young and Rose (2006) found candlestick strategies "do not have value" for DJIA stocks over 1992–2002. Marshall, Young and Cahan (2008) found no evidence candlestick strategies add value in Japanese equities over 1975–2004. Lu and co-authors (2015) found some three-day reversal patterns profitable under one holding rule after costs, not under another. A 2020 forex study found piercing-line and dark-cloud patterns profitable in 14 of 24 pairs and unprofitable in US-dollar pairs.

strategies.platform_testability: TradingView has built-in candlestick pattern detection indicators.
strategies.data_requirement: OHLC data only, with a consistent session close.
sources: Marshall, Young & Rose (2006), Journal of Banking & Finance 30(8)

step_by_step.title: Only look for patterns at meaningful locations
step_by_step.detail: A hammer or engulfing candle in the middle of a random range means almost nothing. The same pattern at a well-tested support or resistance level, after an extended move, is what actually matters.

step_by_step.title: Learn the hammer/pin bar shape precisely
step_by_step.detail: A small body near the top of the range, a long lower wick at least twice the body size, and little to no upper wick. It shows sellers pushed price down hard, then buyers fiercely rejected that and pushed it back up.

step_by_step.title: Learn the engulfing shape precisely
step_by_step.detail: A two-candle pattern: a smaller candle followed by a larger opposite-coloured candle whose BODY fully covers the first candle's body (wicks don't count). A bullish engulfing after a decline, opening below and closing above the first candle's range, shows buyers have taken firm control.

step_by_step.title: Wait for the pattern to fully close before acting
step_by_step.detail: Never pre-empt a hammer or engulfing candle while it's still forming intrabar — it can completely change shape by the close.

step_by_step.title: Check for a volume increase on the pattern candle
step_by_step.detail: A reversal candle on above-average volume is more trustworthy than the identical shape on thin volume.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the open of the next candle, not the pattern candle
step_by_step.detail: Let the pattern candle close first, then take your entry on the following candle's open.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop at the extreme of the pattern
step_by_step.detail: For a bullish hammer or engulfing, stop just below the lowest wick of the pattern. For a bearish version, just above the highest wick.

step_by_step.title: Don't trade every pattern you see — rank them
step_by_step.detail: A pattern at a major, well-tested level after a strong decline, with volume, confirmed by a second candle closing in your direction, is a much stronger signal than a lone pattern with none of that context around it.

strategies.name: Fibonacci Retracement Basics
strategies.summary_one_line: Draws ratio-based levels (38.2%, 50%, 61.8%) across a prior swing to estimate where a pullback might pause.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn how Fibonacci retracement levels are drawn and how traders use them to plan pullback entries.
strategies.core_concept: Pullbacks in trends often retrace a portion of the prior move. Fibonacci ratios provide standard reference points. Their popularity may create some self-fulfilling attention, but there's no established mechanism behind the ratios themselves.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Levels at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50% (not a true Fibonacci ratio, but conventional), 61.8% and 78.6%. Extensions at 127.2% and 161.8%.

rules.entry: In an uptrend, draw from swing low to swing high and look for long entries near 38.2–61.8% with a confirmation candle.
rules.exit: The prior high or an extension.

asset_class_notes.forex: Widely used in FX community analysis.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Equally applicable, but swing-point choice dominates results.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Very widely used in crypto community analysis.
asset_class_notes.futures: Applicable the same way as stocks.

market_conditions.struggles: Ranges or V-shaped moves, where levels are arbitrary.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Choosing swing anchors after the fact.

common_pitfalls: Choosing swing anchors after the fact.
With five levels, price will "respect" one of them by chance (a multiple-target illusion).
strategies.win_rate_note: Claims that "price respects the golden ratio" are common and unsupported. The many levels make any retrospective chart look like a confirmation.

evidence.summary: No robust peer-reviewed evidence that Fibonacci levels predict reversals better than arbitrary levels.

strategies.platform_testability: Built-in Fib Retracement drawing tool on TradingView. Hard to automate without objective swing rules.

image.caption: Fibonacci retracement levels drawn across a fabricated swing.

step_by_step.title: Confirm there's a clear, clean swing to measure
step_by_step.detail: You need an obvious, unambiguous move from a swing low to a swing high (uptrend) or high to low (downtrend). If you can't agree with yourself on where the swing starts and ends, the whole exercise is already on shaky ground.

step_by_step.title: Select the Fibonacci retracement tool
step_by_step.detail: On TradingView, it's in the left-hand drawing toolbar, or search "Fib Retracement" — most charting platforms have an equivalent.

step_by_step.title: Anchor it correctly for the trend direction
step_by_step.detail: Uptrend: click at the swing LOW, drag to the swing HIGH. Downtrend: click at the swing HIGH, drag to the swing LOW. Getting this backwards flips every level to the wrong side of price.

step_by_step.title: Note the key levels it draws
step_by_step.detail: 23.6%, 38.2%, 50% (not a true Fibonacci ratio, but universally included anyway), 61.8% — the "golden ratio", usually treated as the most significant — and 78.6%.

step_by_step.title: Look for confluence, not the Fibonacci level alone
step_by_step.detail: A 61.8% retracement that also lines up with a prior support/resistance level, a moving average, or a trendline is a much stronger area of interest than a bare Fibonacci number with nothing else backing it up.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a confirming candle at the level
step_by_step.detail: Same as any other support/resistance trade: don't buy the instant price touches 61.8%. Wait for a rejection candle or other sign that buyers or sellers are genuinely stepping in there.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop beyond the next level down
step_by_step.detail: Commonly just past 78.6%, or beyond the full swing origin if you want more room to be wrong.

step_by_step.title: Use extensions for targets beyond the prior high or low
step_by_step.detail: If price breaks past where the swing started, the 127.2% and 161.8% extension levels give you a next reference point for taking profit, since there's no prior price history to lean on out there.

videos.title: Fibonacci retracements explained: A step-by-step guide for traders
videos.note: Clean, practical, and focuses on the anchoring step beginners most often get backwards.

strategies.name: Basic Chart Patterns (Double Top/Bottom, Triangles)
strategies.summary_one_line: Recognises classic shapes: a double top or bottom suggests a reversal, and a triangle suggests consolidation before a breakout.
strategies.public_teaser: Learn the classic double top, double bottom and triangle patterns and how their breakout levels are defined.
strategies.core_concept: Patterns are visual summaries of failed tests (double tops/bottoms) or narrowing volatility (triangles). Confirmation comes from a break of the "neckline" or the triangle boundary.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price chart. Optional volume. Measured-move projection equals the pattern height.

rules.entry: Double top: sell on a close below the neckline. Triangles: trade the close through a boundary.
rules.exit: The pattern height projected from the breakout point.
rules.stop: Above the right peak (double top) or inside the pattern (triangle).

asset_class_notes.forex: Patterns appear but fail often in thin liquidity.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Patterns appear but fail often in thin liquidity.
asset_class_notes.futures: Contract rolls can distort pattern geometry on non-adjusted charts.

market_conditions.works_best: Transitional phases between trend and range.
market_conditions.struggles: Choppy, directionless conditions.
market_conditions.failure_modes: False breakouts and patterns that "morph" into other patterns.

common_pitfalls: Ignoring the base rate (most "double tops" never confirm).
strategies.win_rate_note: Pattern-statistics books and sites publish success rates that are often not independently replicated. Treat any quoted success percentage as unverified.

evidence.summary: Lo, Mamaysky and Wang (2000) automated detection of ten patterns, including double tops and bottoms and triangles, on US stocks from 1962 to 1996, and found some patterns provide incremental information about returns — distinct from showing profit after costs.

strategies.platform_testability: TradingView offers auto chart-pattern tools on some plans.
sources: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000), Journal of Finance 55(4)

image.caption: A fabricated double-top pattern with its neckline marked.

step_by_step.title: Learn the double top/bottom shape precisely
step_by_step.detail: Double top: two peaks at roughly the same price, separated by a pullback, forming an "M" shape, usually after an uptrend. Double bottom: the mirror image, a "W" shape, usually after a downtrend.

step_by_step.title: Check the two peaks or troughs are genuinely close in price
step_by_step.detail: If the second peak is meaningfully higher or lower than the first, it's probably not a real double top/bottom — it might just be ongoing trend continuation.

step_by_step.title: Watch volume on the second peak or trough
step_by_step.detail: Classically, volume is expected to be lower on the second peak of a double top than the first — read as a sign of weakening buying pressure.

step_by_step.title: Find the neckline
step_by_step.detail: For a double top, it's the low point of the pullback between the two peaks. For a double bottom, it's the high point of the bounce between the two troughs.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a confirmed close through the neckline
step_by_step.detail: The pattern isn't valid, and shouldn't be traded, until price actually closes through the neckline — not just approaches it.

step_by_step.title: Measure the pattern height for your target
step_by_step.detail: Take the distance from the peak (or trough) to the neckline, then project that same distance beyond the breakout point. That's your measured-move target.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop beyond the pattern's extreme
step_by_step.detail: For a double top, just above the highest peak. For a double bottom, just below the lowest trough.

step_by_step.title: Apply the same logic to triangles
step_by_step.detail: Ascending, descending and symmetrical triangles compress volatility the same way a Bollinger squeeze does. Draw the two converging boundary lines, wait for a confirmed close outside one of them (ideally with volume), and project the widest part of the triangle from the breakout point for your target.

videos.note: Walks through the neckline and measured-move logic clearly, step by step, for a genuine beginner.

strategies.name: Wyckoff Method (Accumulation/Distribution, Springs, Upthrusts)
strategies.summary_one_line: Reads large operators' footprints through repeating accumulation and distribution phases.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore Richard Wyckoff's framework for reading supply, demand and phases of accumulation and distribution.
strategies.core_concept: Developed by Richard Wyckoff in the early 1900s. It rests on three laws: supply and demand, cause and effect (the range "builds a cause" for the later move), and effort versus result (volume versus price progress). The "Composite Man" heuristic imagines a single large operator. Phases A–E describe the schematic: accumulation includes the preliminary support, selling climax (SC), automatic rally (AR), secondary test (ST), Spring, sign of strength (SOS) and last point of support (LPS); distribution mirrors this with the buying climax (BC), upthrust after distribution (UTAD) and sign of weakness (SOW).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price and real volume, optional point-and-figure for "cause" counts, and relative strength versus the index.

rules.entry: Long on a Spring (a brief break below range support that quickly reclaims it) or on a test, or on the LPS after the SOS. Mirror the logic in distribution with an upthrust/UTAD for shorts.
rules.exit: A point-and-figure count or the next resistance.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Best suited because of centralised volume.
asset_class_notes.futures: Best suited because of centralised volume.
asset_class_notes.forex: Only tick volume is available, a weak proxy — a Federal Reserve IFDP paper notes quote-frequency measures "have clearly been poor substitutes" for actual FX volume.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Volume is fragmented across exchanges, and wash trading has been a documented concern.

market_conditions.struggles: Labelling which phase you're in is ambiguous in real time.
market_conditions.failure_modes: "Springs" that turn into breakdowns rather than reversals.

common_pitfalls: Forcing every range into a schematic.
Using forex tick volume as if it were real volume.
strategies.win_rate_note: Course marketing often highlights perfectly annotated past schematics. Real-time ambiguity means there's no reliable profile of how often it wins. Spring entries offer tight stops, so a favourable reward-to-risk appearance is common, but how often they actually work is unknown.

evidence.summary: No rigorous peer-reviewed predictive test was found. The literature is descriptive (e.g. Hank Pruden's work) or about AI phase classification, which measures detection accuracy rather than return prediction.

strategies.platform_testability: Mostly manual on TradingView, though community Wyckoff scripts exist.
sources: StockCharts ChartSchool, "The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial"
Pruden, "The Three Skills of Top Trading"

strategies.name: Volume Spread Analysis (VSA)
strategies.summary_one_line: Interprets each bar's spread (range), close location and volume to infer professional buying or selling.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Volume Spread Analysis interprets the relationship between bar range, closing position and volume.
strategies.core_concept: Developed by Tom Williams from Wyckoff ideas. Signals include "no demand" (an up bar on narrow spread with low volume), "stopping volume", "test" and "upthrust". The core idea is effort versus result.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Bar chart with volume and a volume moving average for relative comparison.

rules.entry: In context (background strength or weakness), a low-volume test after stopping volume prompts a long (mirror for shorts).
rules.exit: On signs of weakness.

asset_class_notes.forex: A contested approximation using tick volume.

market_conditions.struggles: News-driven moves, where readings are contradictory.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Over-reading a single bar out of context.

strategies.win_rate_note: Vendor software and courses imply that "professional money" can be read reliably from single bars. This is unsupported.

evidence.summary: No peer-reviewed test identified. Lo, Mamaysky and Wang reported that volume trends added little information when combined with technical patterns.

strategies.platform_testability: Community VSA scripts on TradingView.

strategies.name: Market Profile / Auction Market Theory
strategies.summary_one_line: Organises price by time spent at each level (TPO), to see where the market finds "fair value" and where it rejects price.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Market Profile organizes trading activity by time at price to describe value and balance.
strategies.core_concept: Developed by J. Peter Steidlmayer at the Chicago Board of Trade in the 1980s. Markets auction to facilitate trade: they move away from balance to find new participants, then rotate. Key elements are the value area (about 70% of TPOs), the point of control, the initial balance (first hour), single prints, and day types (normal, trend, double distribution).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: 30-minute TPO periods; value area 70%; initial balance = first 60 minutes of the regular session.

rules.entry: The "80% rule": if price opens outside the prior value area and re-enters it for two TPO periods, traders look for a traverse to the other side. Also: initial-balance breakouts on trend days.
rules.exit: The other side of value, or a trend-day target.

asset_class_notes.futures: Designed for futures (especially CME index and rate futures) with defined sessions.
asset_class_notes.forex: No natural session, so session choice is arbitrary.
asset_class_notes.crypto: No natural session, so session choice is arbitrary.

market_conditions.struggles: Trend days, where fading value fails.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Treating the "80% rule" as a literal probability.

common_pitfalls: Treating the "80% rule" as literal probability.
strategies.win_rate_note: The "80% rule" name itself implies a specific success rate. Flag it as a heuristic label, not a tested probability.

evidence.summary: Little rigorous testing. The CME Group has historically provided educational material explaining the method, which doesn't show it works.

strategies.platform_testability: TradingView offers TPO charts on paid plans.
strategies.data_requirement: Intraday data and a defined session.
sources: CME Group education on Market Profile

strategies.name: Volume Profile (POC, Value Area, HVN/LVN)
strategies.summary_one_line: Plots traded volume at each price to find high-volume "acceptance" and low-volume "rejection" areas.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Volume Profile maps where trading activity concentrated and how traders reference those levels.
strategies.core_concept: High-volume nodes (HVN) act as magnets or balance areas; low-volume nodes (LVN) are where price moved through quickly and may move quickly again. The point of control (POC) is the single price with the most volume, and the value area is about 70% of volume.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Session, visible-range or fixed-range profile; 70% value area.

rules.entry: Fade moves into HVNs or the POC in balance; expect fast travel through LVNs. Take breakouts from value with acceptance outside it.
rules.exit: The opposing node or value edge.

asset_class_notes.forex: Tick-volume profiles are a proxy; some traders use CME FX futures volume instead.

market_conditions.struggles: News-driven repricing.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Choosing the anchor range after the fact.

common_pitfalls: Choosing the anchor range after the fact.
strategies.win_rate_note: Marketed as "institutional levels". Unverified.

evidence.summary: No robust independent tests of profile-based trading rules were identified.

strategies.platform_testability: Built-in volume profile tools on TradingView (some on paid tiers).

strategies.name: Order Flow / Footprint Charts / Delta
strategies.summary_one_line: Looks inside each bar at aggressive buying versus selling (bid/ask volume, delta, imbalances, absorption).
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how footprint charts and delta break down buying and selling activity inside each price bar.
strategies.core_concept: Price moves when aggressive orders overwhelm resting liquidity. Signals include stacked imbalances, absorption (heavy aggression without price progress), delta divergence and exhaustion. Order flow is well established academically as a driver of price — Evans and Lyons' widely cited FX research tied inter-dealer order flow to exchange-rate moves — but that's different from showing retail footprint-pattern rules are profitable.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Footprint/cluster charts, cumulative delta, DOM (Level 2), time and sales.

rules.entry: At a key level, absorption plus a delta flip leads to an entry in the absorbing side's direction.
rules.exit: The next liquidity area.
rules.stop: A few ticks beyond the absorption level.

asset_class_notes.futures: The natural home, because centralised exchanges publish trades with the aggressor side.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Fragmented across venues, so footprint data is partial.
asset_class_notes.forex: No consolidated tape, so this isn't truly possible on spot — CME FX futures are used as a proxy.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Per-exchange data is available but fragmented.

market_conditions.works_best: Liquid, active sessions (e.g. the US cash open for index futures).
market_conditions.struggles: Thin markets and around news.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Spoofing/iceberg orders distort the read.

common_pitfalls: Treating DOM orders as firm (they can be pulled).
High costs per trade relative to the targets.
strategies.win_rate_note: Scalping styles often show a high proportion of winners with small targets. Fees and slippage decide the real outcome. Flag "90% scalper" claims.

evidence.summary: Strong academic evidence that order flow moves prices. No independent evidence that retail footprint setups are profitable after costs. Base rates for day traders are poor (97% of persistent Brazilian futures day traders lost money).

strategies.platform_testability: TradingView has volume footprint on higher plans; specialist platforms (Sierra Chart, ATAS, Bookmap) are commonly used.
strategies.data_requirement: Tick-level data with aggressor flags; a futures data subscription.
sources: CME Group education on order types and market depth
Evans & Lyons (2002), Journal of Political Economy

strategies.name: Anchored VWAP Strategies
strategies.summary_one_line: Starts a volume-weighted average price from a chosen event (earnings, a swing low, a gap) to estimate participants' average cost since that event.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how anchored VWAP measures the average traded price since a chosen event and how traders reference it.
strategies.core_concept: Popularised by Brian Shannon. Since an event, the anchored VWAP shows whether buyers (or sellers) are, on average, in profit. Reclaims and losses of the line mark shifts in control. VWAP is genuinely used by institutions as an execution benchmark, but that doesn't make it a predictive level.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: VWAP anchored at a significant bar, with optional standard-deviation bands.

rules.entry: In an uptrend, buy a pullback that holds the anchored VWAP from the last major low.
rules.exit: A loss of the line suggests a regime change.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Main use is around earnings and gaps.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy markets, which cause repeated crosses.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Anchoring to the "perfect" bar after the fact.

common_pitfalls: Anchoring to the "perfect" bar after the fact.
Using too many anchors, so one will always "work".
strategies.win_rate_note: No credible data exists on how often this wins. The profile depends on whether it's used for trend or reversion.

evidence.summary: No peer-reviewed tests of anchored VWAP rules were identified.

strategies.platform_testability: Built-in Anchored VWAP tool on TradingView.
sources: Shannon, "Maximum Trading Gains with Anchored VWAP"

image.caption: Synthetic price with a volume-weighted average price line anchored from the start of the move.

strategies.name: ICT / Smart Money Concepts (Order Blocks, Liquidity Sweeps, Fair Value Gaps)
strategies.summary_one_line: A retail framework that interprets charts as the footprints of "smart money" engineering liquidity.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the vocabulary of Smart Money Concepts, including order blocks, liquidity sweeps and fair value gaps, and the debate around them.
strategies.core_concept: Popularised online by Michael J. Huddleston ("Inner Circle Trader") and many derivative educators. Its claim is that large players run stops above and below obvious highs and lows ("liquidity"), then reverse. Key terms: order block (the last opposing candle before an impulsive move), fair value gap/FVG (a three-candle imbalance), break of structure / change of character, and session "kill zones" (time windows like the London and New York opens). "Premium/discount" is defined by a 50% retracement of the range.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price only, with session times.

rules.entry: Wait for a liquidity sweep of a prior high or low, then a market structure shift on a lower timeframe, then enter on a retrace into the FVG or order block.
rules.exit: Opposing liquidity.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Less commonly applied, but the same vocabulary is used.

market_conditions.works_best: Advocates apply it everywhere, which is itself a warning sign of unfalsifiability.
market_conditions.struggles: Deep, multi-venue markets, where no single entity engineers price — the "institutional" story is least plausible there.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Sweeps that continue rather than reverse.

strategies.win_rate_note: "Sniper entries" and huge reward-to-risk screenshots are pervasive in this space and are unsupported. Treat any claim that this setup wins most of the time and pays several R with real caution.

evidence.summary: No peer-reviewed test of ICT/SMC was identified. One vendor-published (not independent) no-lookahead backtest of a sweep-then-structure-shift-then-FVG entry on EURUSD one-minute data (2019–2025) reported negative expectancy (about −0.27 to −0.35R). The same source notes the visual three-candle FVG "is a charting heuristic with no peer-reviewed test". The concepts overlap with older ideas (stop runs, supply/demand, Wyckoff springs).

strategies.platform_testability: Many community TradingView scripts plot order blocks and FVGs, with inconsistent definitions.
sources: TradingView Education (community SMC ideas, labelled as community content)
CFTC customer advisory, "There's Nothing to Like About Scammers on Social Media"
Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti (2020) for base rates

strategies.name: Elliott Wave Theory
strategies.summary_one_line: Sees prices moving in fractal patterns of five waves with the trend and three against it.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore R.N. Elliott's wave principle, its counting rules, and why wave counts are debated.
strategies.core_concept: From Ralph Nelson Elliott (1930s), popularised by Frost and Prechter. Crowd psychology is said to produce repeating 5-3 structures at all degrees. Three hard rules apply in impulses: wave 2 never retraces more than 100% of wave 1, wave 3 is never the shortest, and wave 4 does not overlap wave 1. Fibonacci ratios are used for projections.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price, Fibonacci tools, and optional oscillators (e.g. MACD for wave 3 or 5 divergence).

rules.entry: At the end of wave 2 (targeting wave 3) or the end of wave 4.
rules.exit: Projected wave targets using Fibonacci extensions.
rules.stop: Where a count rule would be broken (e.g. below the start of wave 1).

asset_class_notes.crypto: Popular, though thin or manipulated markets create irregular structures.

market_conditions.struggles: Corrective structures (zigzags, flats, triangles, combinations) allow many alternative counts.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Re-counting after failure, which makes the method hard to falsify.

strategies.win_rate_note: Accuracy claims are usually based on cherry-picked successful counts. The rule-based invalidation points do give a defined risk, which is its most useful practical feature regardless of forecasting accuracy.

evidence.summary: Supportive papers exist mainly in low-tier venues and are retrospective — e.g. D'Angelo and Grimaldi (2017) on EUR/USD claimed the 2009–2015 exchange rate "could be forecasted with great accuracy". AI papers measure wave-recognition accuracy rather than out-of-sample trading results. No rigorous, data-snooping-robust evidence of profitability was found.

strategies.platform_testability: Elliott Wave drawing tools are built into TradingView, plus community auto-count scripts. Hard to automate objectively.

image.caption: A schematic five-wave impulse followed by a corrective move, labelled 0 through C.

strategies.name: Harmonic Patterns (Gartley, Bat, Butterfly, Crab)
strategies.summary_one_line: Identifies five-point XABCD structures whose legs match specific Fibonacci ratios, pointing to a "potential reversal zone" (PRZ).
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the XABCD harmonic patterns and how their Fibonacci ratio rules are defined.
strategies.core_concept: Developed from H.M. Gartley (1935) and later Scott Carney and Larry Pesavento. Typical definitions: Gartley (B at 61.8% of XA, D at 78.6%), Bat (B at 38.2–50%, D at 88.6%), Butterfly (B at 78.6%, D at 127–161.8%), Crab (D at 161.8% of XA).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: XABCD drawing tool, Fibonacci ratios, tolerance bands.

rules.entry: In the PRZ at point D with a confirmation candle.
rules.exit: 38.2% and 61.8% retracements of the AD leg.
rules.stop: Beyond the PRZ or point X.

asset_class_notes.crypto: Also very popular, though volatility strains the ratio tolerances.

market_conditions.works_best: Ranges and trend exhaustion, per advocates.
market_conditions.struggles: Strong trends, where price drives through the PRZ.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Tolerances so loose that patterns appear everywhere.

common_pitfalls: Tolerances so loose that patterns are everywhere.
Ignoring how rarely strict patterns actually complete.
strategies.win_rate_note: Broker and education sites publish figures such as ">85%" or ">70%" with no independent basis. Treat this as a strategy where high-success claims are common but unverified.

evidence.summary: Very limited. de Souza, Ribeiro and Suarez (2021, Latin American Journal of Development) studied forex and noted the patterns' frequency is reported "from unverified sources", concluding that "only one of the popular patterns has a probability of occurrence beyond the trivial" — and that tested occurrence, not profitability.

strategies.platform_testability: XABCD drawing tool built into TradingView, plus community auto-detection.

strategies.name: Gann Methods (Angles, Square of Nine, Time Cycles)
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses geometric angles, numerical squares and time cycles attributed to W.D. Gann to forecast support, resistance and turning dates.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore W.D. Gann's angles, squares and time cycles and the long-running debate about them.
strategies.core_concept: Price and time are said to be linked. The 1×1 angle represents one unit of price per unit of time. The Square of Nine maps numbers onto a spiral. Anniversary and cycle dates are used for timing. Many claims derive from Gann's own marketing in the early 20th century.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Gann fan, box and square tools. The choice of price-to-time scaling is critical and arbitrary.

rules.entry: Price above the 1×1 angle from a major low is read as bullish; breaks of angles signal a shift to the next angle.
rules.exit: Time cycles are used to anticipate reversal dates.

market_conditions.works_best: Undefined — the method is flexible enough to "fit" most histories.
market_conditions.struggles: Any condition, given the lack of a defined edge.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Arbitrary scaling and selective anchoring producing whatever result is wanted.

common_pitfalls: Mysticism and astrology overlap in some sub-schools.
strategies.win_rate_note: Legendary-accuracy stories circulating about this method are unverified historical marketing.

evidence.summary: An independent, non-peer-reviewed 2026 SSRN working paper (Brown, "Do Gann Angles Work?") pre-registered hypotheses on 2,491 sessions of E-mini S&P 500 one-minute bars (2016–2025). It found fan crossings on the 1×2, 2×1 and 1×1 angles "produce significantly negative net returns in both periods". A strict steepness hierarchy "finds no support". Only a separate "dynamic price anchors" construct showed a positive effect.

strategies.platform_testability: Gann tools are built into TradingView.

strategies.name: Fibonacci Confluence / Clustering
strategies.summary_one_line: Looks for price zones where several Fibonacci retracements and extensions from different swings overlap, and treats them as higher-interest areas.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders combine multiple Fibonacci measurements to find overlapping zones of interest.
strategies.core_concept: Clustering of independent measurements is said to strengthen a level. Statistically, more lines raise the chance of a coincidental "hit".
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Multiple retracements and extensions (e.g. 61.8% of the large swing plus 127.2% of the smaller swing), and time Fibonacci.

rules.entry: At the cluster, with confirmation.
rules.exit: The prior swing.

asset_class_notes.forex: Universal use; results depend on swing selection.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Universal use; results depend on swing selection.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Universal use; results depend on swing selection.
asset_class_notes.futures: Universal use; results depend on swing selection.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy data, where clusters appear everywhere.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Retrospective anchoring to make a cluster appear meaningful.

strategies.win_rate_note: Marketed as identifying "high-probability zones". Unsupported.

evidence.summary: None robust identified.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual Fibonacci tools on TradingView.

strategies.name: Cycle Analysis (Hurst Cycles, Dominant Cycle Tools)
strategies.summary_one_line: Assumes prices contain repeating, roughly regular cycles and tries to time troughs and peaks.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how cycle analysts look for recurring rhythms in price and the limits of that approach.
strategies.core_concept: J.M. Hurst's "Profit Magic of Stock Transaction Timing" (1970) proposed nested, harmonically related cycles. Modern tools (e.g. John Ehlers' DSP indicators) estimate a "dominant cycle".
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Detrended Price Oscillator, Hurst cycle envelopes, Ehlers indicators, spectral analysis.

rules.entry: Buy near projected cycle troughs that are confirmed by price.
rules.exit: Near the projected crest.

asset_class_notes.commodities: Agricultural futures' seasonal cycles are a distinct and better-grounded idea.
asset_class_notes.crypto: A short history limits cycle estimates.

market_conditions.works_best: Regular, stable cycle environments (per the theory).
market_conditions.struggles: Cycles that shift in length and amplitude.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Phase drift — the dominant failure mode.

strategies.win_rate_note: No credible profile of how often this wins exists.

evidence.summary: Little independent trading-rule evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: DPO is built into TradingView; Hurst and Ehlers tools are community scripts.

strategies.name: Ichimoku Kinko Hyo (Advanced Use)
strategies.summary_one_line: A multi-line Japanese system that shows trend, momentum, and support/resistance through a "cloud".
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how the Ichimoku system's lines and cloud are combined to frame trend and equilibrium.
strategies.core_concept: Developed by Goichi Hosoda (published 1969). Midpoint-based lines reflect equilibrium. Advanced use adds Hosoda's time theory and wave/price-target principles beyond the basic signals.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Tenkan 9, Kijun 26, Senkou B 52, with a 26-period displacement.

rules.entry: Long when price is above the cloud, Tenkan is above Kijun, Chikou is above price from 26 periods ago, and the future cloud is bullish.
rules.exit: A Kijun break or a close back into the cloud.

asset_class_notes.crypto: Popular; some traders change settings for 24/7 markets.

market_conditions.struggles: A flat or thin cloud, which gives whipsaws.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Too many conditions, so signals arrive late.

common_pitfalls: Too many conditions, so signals arrive late.
strategies.win_rate_note: A trend-following profile. Claims of a "complete system" overstate what's actually been tested.

evidence.summary: Limited peer-reviewed testing. Generic trend-following evidence applies at the category level only.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

strategies.name: Renko, Kagi and Point-and-Figure Charting
strategies.summary_one_line: Chart types that ignore time and plot only meaningful price moves, which filters out noise.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore time-independent chart types that only plot price changes beyond a set size.
strategies.core_concept: By plotting only moves of a set size (a Renko brick, or a P&F box with a 3-box reversal), trends and breakouts appear cleaner. P&F has a long history in US equities (e.g. Dorsey Wright's work) and supports "vertical count" price objectives.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Renko: brick size from ATR(14), or fixed. P&F: box size by price scale or percentage, 3-box reversal. Kagi: reversal amount.

rules.entry: P&F: buy on a double-top breakout (an X column exceeds the prior X column). Renko: trade a brick colour change (e.g. two bricks).
rules.exit: The P&F vertical count target, or a brick-colour reversal.
rules.stop: At the reversal (P&F) or recent brick extreme (Renko).

market_conditions.struggles: Ranges, which create flip-flopping bricks.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Unrealistic backtests on Renko, since brick formation can use data not available in real time ("repainting").

strategies.win_rate_note: Renko backtests often show an unrealistically high proportion of winning trades because of construction artefacts — flag this explicitly to anyone using Renko to backtest.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Renko, Kagi and P&F chart types are built into TradingView. Use caution with strategy testing on non-standard charts.
sources: du Plessis, "The Definitive Guide to Point and Figure"
TradingView Help on non-standard chart backtesting

strategies.name: Turtle Trading / Donchian Channel Breakout System
strategies.summary_one_line: A complete rule set teaching novice traders (the "Turtles", 1983) to buy new highs and sell new lows, with volatility-based sizing.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the rule set behind the famous Turtle experiment, including breakouts, volatility sizing and exits.
strategies.core_concept: Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt's experiment in whether trading could be taught, building on Richard Donchian's channel. The edge, if any, comes from capturing rare large trends across many markets while limiting losses.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: System 1: enter on a 20-day breakout, exit on a 10-day opposite breakout, skip the next signal after a win, with a 55-day failsafe. System 2: enter on a 55-day breakout, exit on a 20-day opposite breakout. N = the 20-day ATR; unit sizing sets 1N of movement to about 1% of equity. Stop at 2N; pyramid every ½N, up to 4 units.

rules.entry: A 20-day (System 1) or 55-day (System 2) breakout.
rules.exit: The opposite N-day breakout.
rules.stop: 2N from entry, trailing with pyramided units.

asset_class_notes.futures: Designed for diversified futures (commodities, rates, currencies, indices).
asset_class_notes.forex: Workable on spot FX, but swap costs matter.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Weaker on single names, because of gaps and lower trend persistence.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy, flat years, where long losing streaks are normal.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Trading only one market (no diversification).

strategies.win_rate_note: A classic design where most individual trades lose money and a few outsized trends pay for all of them. Any claim that a Turtle-style system wins most of its trades misunderstands how it's built.

evidence.summary: Breakout rules are a form of time-series momentum. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) and Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen (2017) document trend premia across many futures markets over long histories. The original Turtle results themselves are anecdotal (accounts of the Turtles' performance) rather than audited, independent research.

strategies.platform_testability: Donchian Channels are built into TradingView; straightforward in Pine Script. Multi-market portfolio testing needs other tools.
strategies.data_requirement: Daily OHLC with continuous futures contracts.
sources: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012), Journal of Financial Economics 104(2)

image.caption: Synthetic price with 20-period Donchian channel highs and lows plotted.

strategies.name: Time-Series Momentum / Volatility-Scaled Trend Following
strategies.summary_one_line: Holds each market long if its past return (e.g. 12 months) is positive and short if negative, sized so each position contributes similar risk.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the systematic trend-following approach studied by academics and used by many managed-futures funds.
strategies.core_concept: Trends persist for months, perhaps because of under-reaction and then over-reaction, along with behavioural biases and non-profit-seeking participants such as central banks and hedgers. Diversifying across dozens of markets is central.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Lookbacks of 1, 3 and 12 months. Volatility targeting (e.g. scaling by inverse ex-ante volatility).

rules.entry: Monthly rebalance; the sign of the past return sets the direction.
rules.exit: Rebalanced out when the sign flips.
rules.stop: Position size is inversely proportional to volatility, acting as the main risk control.

asset_class_notes.futures: Core use: equity index, bond, currency and commodity futures.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Shows strong trends but has a short history.

market_conditions.struggles: Sharp reversals and trendless years.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Under-diversification and leverage misuse.

strategies.win_rate_note: A low-to-moderate proportion of trades win, with positive skew and long drawdowns — the same shape as other trend-following systems.

evidence.summary: Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012) found time-series momentum in all 58 instruments tested. Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen (2017) found positive returns in each decade since 1880. Kim, Tse and Wald (2016) find that "without scaling by volatility, time series momentum and a buy-and-hold strategy offer similar cumulative returns, and their alphas are not significantly different."

strategies.platform_testability: Single-market logic can be built in Pine Script; portfolio implementation needs external tools.
sources: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017), Journal of Portfolio Management 44(1)
Kim, Tse & Wald (2016), Journal of Financial Markets

strategies.name: Connors RSI-2 and Short-Term Mean-Reversion Systems
strategies.summary_one_line: Buys short, sharp pullbacks in long-term uptrends using an ultra-short 2-period RSI, and exits on a quick bounce.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore Larry Connors' short-term pullback framework based on a 2-period RSI and a long-term trend filter.
strategies.core_concept: In equity indices, very short-term declines within uptrends have historically tended to partially reverse. This links to the academic "short-term reversal" effect in stocks, documented by Jegadeesh (1990) and Lehmann.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: 200-day SMA, RSI(2), 5-day SMA. A related "ConnorsRSI" composite combines RSI(3), streak RSI(2) and percent rank (100).

rules.entry: Price closes above the 200-day SMA, and RSI(2) closes below 5 (or 10) — buy at the close.
rules.exit: A close above the 5-day SMA. Connors' published work argued against stop-losses in this system.
rules.stop: None in the original design (a known weakness, see pitfalls).

asset_class_notes.stocks: Designed for US index ETFs and liquid stocks.
asset_class_notes.forex: Results in practitioner tests are inconsistent.

market_conditions.struggles: Crash regimes, where dips keep falling (e.g. 2008, 2020).
market_conditions.failure_modes: No-stop designs that create large losses in a crash.

common_pitfalls: Ignoring the decay in short-term reversal as markets became faster.
strategies.win_rate_note: A textbook high-proportion-of-winners, negative-skew design: many small wins, occasional large losses. Practitioner backtests on SPY show sizeable drawdowns (one widely cited commercial backtest reports a maximum drawdown of 34% while invested only 28% of the time). Treat any "wins almost every time" headline for this strategy with real caution.

evidence.summary: Connors' own books are the primary sources, and most replication comes from commercial blogs. No rigorous peer-reviewed out-of-sample test of RSI-2 itself was identified. The underlying short-term reversal effect is academically documented.

strategies.platform_testability: Built-in indicators make it easy in Pine Script.
sources: Connors & Alvarez, "Short Term Trading Strategies That Work"

strategies.name: Elder Triple Screen
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses three "screens": a longer timeframe for trend, an intermediate oscillator for pullbacks, and a short-term trigger for entry.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore Dr. Alexander Elder's three-screen process for aligning trend, pullback and entry timing.
strategies.core_concept: From Alexander Elder's "Trading for a Living" (1993). Trend indicators and oscillators contradict each other, so use each on its proper timeframe.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Screen 1 (weekly): MACD histogram slope or 13-week EMA. Screen 2 (daily): Force Index (2-day EMA) or Stochastic/Williams %R. Screen 3: a trailing buy-stop above the prior day's high.

rules.entry: In a weekly uptrend, wait for a daily oscillator dip, then enter on a break of the prior day's high.
rules.exit: Elder's "2% rule" (maximum risk per trade) and "6% rule" (maximum monthly drawdown) govern when to step back.

asset_class_notes.forex: Usable with the same weekly/daily/intraday structure.
asset_class_notes.stocks: Usable with the same weekly/daily/intraday structure.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Usable with the same weekly/daily/intraday structure.
asset_class_notes.futures: Usable with the same weekly/daily/intraday structure.

market_conditions.struggles: Major turning points.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Timeframe mismatch between the screens.

strategies.win_rate_note: A moderate profile. No credible published figures on how often it wins exist.

evidence.summary: No independent tests identified.

strategies.platform_testability: Multi-timeframe indicators work in Pine Script (request.security).
sources: Elder, "Trading for a Living"/"The New Trading for a Living"
StockCharts ChartSchool, "Elder Triple Screen Trading System"

strategies.name: TTM Squeeze / Bollinger–Keltner Squeeze
strategies.summary_one_line: Flags periods when Bollinger Bands contract inside Keltner Channels (a volatility "squeeze"), then trades the release in the direction of momentum.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders identify volatility compression using Bollinger Bands and Keltner Channels.
strategies.core_concept: Volatility mean-reverts: quiet periods tend to be followed by expansion. John Carter popularised the TTM Squeeze, with a momentum histogram for direction.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: BB(20, 2), Keltner(20, 1.5×ATR), and a linear-regression momentum histogram.

rules.entry: The squeeze is "on" when the BB are inside the KC; enter when it "fires" (BB exit KC) in the histogram's direction.
rules.exit: Momentum fading (e.g. two histogram bars shrinking) or a trailing stop.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Popular here, plus options and index futures.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Squeezes around news can fire both ways.
asset_class_notes.forex: Squeezes around news can fire both ways.

market_conditions.struggles: False fires are common.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Assuming direction from the squeeze itself before it fires.

common_pitfalls: Assuming direction from the squeeze itself.
strategies.win_rate_note: A breakout-style profile. Vendor marketing for this specific setup has historically been aggressive about claimed results.

evidence.summary: The fact that volatility clusters and mean-reverts is well established. Directional profitability of squeeze rules specifically is not independently established.

strategies.platform_testability: TTM-style squeeze scripts are widely available on TradingView (community).
sources: StockCharts ChartSchool, "Keltner Channels" and "Bollinger Band Squeeze"

strategies.name: Pairs Trading / Statistical Arbitrage Basics
strategies.summary_one_line: Goes long one asset and short a closely related one when their price relationship diverges, and closes when it converges.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how pairs trading looks at the relationship between two related assets rather than the direction of one.
strategies.core_concept: Two economically linked instruments' prices (normalised, or with a cointegrated spread) tend to revert after divergence. The strategy aims to be market-neutral.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Distance method (Gatev and co-authors): a 12-month formation period, picking pairs with the minimum squared distance between normalised prices, opening at a 2-standard-deviation divergence. Alternatives: cointegration (Engle-Granger) and z-score of the spread.

rules.entry: A 2-standard-deviation divergence between the pair.
rules.exit: The spread crossing back to its mean, or a time stop.
