rules.stop: A "relationship break" stop if the spread never converges.

asset_class_notes.stocks: The classic use — same-sector stocks and share classes.
asset_class_notes.futures: Calendar spreads and related commodities, e.g. crude versus products.
asset_class_notes.forex: Correlated currency pairs, though less stable.

market_conditions.struggles: A structural break (mergers, fundamentals), where the spread never converges.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Confusing correlation with cointegration.

strategies.win_rate_note: Often a high proportion of winning trades with rare large losses from relationship breaks.

evidence.summary: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) studied US stocks from 1962 to 2002 and found "average annualized excess returns of up to 11%" for self-financing portfolios of pairs, with profits "typically exceeding conservative transaction-cost estimates". Their working paper noted part of the profits may be due to market microstructure effects.

strategies.platform_testability: TradingView supports spread charts (e.g. "AAPL/MSFT"), and z-scores are doable in Pine Script. Proper pair selection needs external tools.
strategies.data_requirement: Data for two instruments plus shorting access.
sources: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst (2006), Review of Financial Studies 19(3)

strategies.name: Intermarket Analysis
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses relationships between bonds, stocks, commodities and the dollar to judge the context and likely leadership for a market.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders compare related markets to understand the broader backdrop for a chart.
strategies.core_concept: Popularised by John Murphy. Markets are linked through rates, inflation and growth (e.g. falling yields support equities, and a rising dollar pressures commodities). The relationships drift over time, and stock–bond correlation has changed sign across eras.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Ratio charts, correlation coefficients, relative strength between assets.

rules.entry: Used as a filter, e.g. favour equity longs when bonds and the advance-decline line confirm.
rules.exit: Leadership rotation read from ratio charts.
rules.stop: Not applicable as a standalone entry system.

asset_class_notes.forex: Commodity currencies versus commodities is a common application.
asset_class_notes.futures: Core use case across rates, commodities and indices.

market_conditions.struggles: Regime changes, which break relationships.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Assuming a fixed correlation sign across eras.

strategies.win_rate_note: Not a standalone entry system, so no meaningful win-count profile applies to it on its own.

evidence.summary: Cross-asset lead-lag relationships are studied academically, but rigorous evidence for retail intermarket trading rules specifically is limited.

strategies.platform_testability: Ratio and correlation tools are built into TradingView.

strategies.name: RSI Divergence
strategies.summary_one_line: Compares RSI swings with price swings to spot weakening momentum.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders compare RSI swings with price swings to spot weakening momentum.
strategies.core_concept: Price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high (bearish divergence), or the reverse (bullish).

rules.entry: On a confirmation break of the swing (a trendline or the prior bar).
rules.exit: At the opposing swing or a target.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Divergences can repeat many times in strong trends.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Divergences can repeat many times in strong trends.

market_conditions.struggles: Strong trends, where divergence can persist through multiple failures.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Trading divergence without a confirming trigger.

strategies.win_rate_note: Marketed as an "early reversal" signal with a high proportion of winners. Unsupported.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Confirm the prevailing trend first
step_by_step.detail: Check a higher timeframe or a moving average to see whether the market is trending up, trending down, or just ranging sideways. Regular RSI divergence is a reversal signal, so it only means something once there's an established trend for it to reverse.

step_by_step.title: Keep RSI on its default 14-period setting
step_by_step.detail: Shorter lengths throw up more divergences, but most of the extra ones are noise. Stick with 14 on whatever timeframe you actually trade — a daily or 4-hour divergence carries far more weight than one on a 5-minute chart.

step_by_step.title: Mark the price's recent swing high or low
step_by_step.detail: For a possible bearish signal, watch for price printing a higher high than its last swing high. For a possible bullish signal, watch for price printing a lower low than its last swing low.

step_by_step.title: Compare that swing to RSI at the same two points
step_by_step.detail: Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high. Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low while RSI makes a higher low. Draw a line connecting the two RSI peaks (or troughs) so the mismatch with price is visible.

step_by_step.title: Treat the divergence as a warning, not a signal on its own
step_by_step.detail: Divergence only tells you that momentum is fading under the current move — it doesn't say when, or if, price will actually turn. It can sit there for many bars before anything happens, or not resolve at all.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a structure break to confirm it
step_by_step.detail: For a bearish setup, wait for price to break a nearby support level, break an up-trendline, or for RSI itself to cross back below 50. For a bullish setup, wait for the mirror image of all three.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the confirmation and set a stop beyond the extreme
step_by_step.detail: Enter once the break happens, not before. Place the stop above the higher high (bearish) or below the lower low (bullish) that created the divergence in the first place — if price reclaims that extreme, the setup is invalidated.

step_by_step.title: Target the start of the prior move or a fixed risk-to-reward multiple
step_by_step.detail: A common target is the point where the move that caused the divergence began, or simply a multiple of your stop distance (e.g. twice the risk) if there's no obvious nearby level.

videos.title: RSI Divergence Trading Strategy: How to Identify and use RSI
videos.note: Walks through spotting bullish and bearish RSI divergence on a live chart and explains why it's read as an early warning on trend reversals, not a standalone signal.

strategies.name: MACD Divergence
strategies.summary_one_line: Watches differences between MACD and price swings as a sign of a momentum shift.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how differences between MACD and price swings are read as momentum shifts.
strategies.core_concept: MACD(12, 26, 9) histogram or line peaks diverging from price.

rules.entry: On confirmation via a signal-line cross or a structure break.
rules.exit: At the opposing swing.

market_conditions.struggles: Strong trends with repeated divergences.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Mixing line versus histogram divergences.

strategies.win_rate_note: No credible data exists on how often this wins.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Set up MACD with its standard inputs
step_by_step.detail: Use the default 12/26/9 settings (fast EMA, slow EMA, signal line) applied to the close. These are what almost every chart platform ships with by default, and what most of the research behind this strategy actually tested.

step_by_step.title: Establish the prevailing trend on a higher timeframe
step_by_step.detail: MACD divergence is a reversal signal, so check a daily or 4-hour chart (or a simple moving average) first to confirm there's an actual trend in place for the divergence to challenge.

step_by_step.title: Mark the price's swing highs or lows
step_by_step.detail: For bearish divergence, look for price making a higher high. For bullish divergence, look for price making a lower low — exactly the same structure as RSI divergence, just read off MACD instead.

step_by_step.title: Compare that swing to the MACD line or histogram
step_by_step.detail: Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high while the MACD line or histogram peaks lower than its previous peak. Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low while MACD's trough is higher than its previous trough.

step_by_step.title: Know the three divergence types you'll actually see
step_by_step.detail: Regular divergence (price extreme vs. MACD extreme, as above) signals a possible reversal. Hidden divergence (the mirror pattern) signals a possible trend continuation instead — don't mix the two up when deciding your bias.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a signal-line cross or a structure break to confirm
step_by_step.detail: Don't act on the divergence itself. Wait for MACD to cross its own signal line in the new direction, or for price to break a nearby support/resistance level or trendline, before treating the divergence as confirmed.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the confirmation bar and place your stop
step_by_step.detail: Enter once confirmed, with a stop beyond the swing high or low that created the divergence — that's the level which, if price reclaims it, tells you the reversal read was wrong.

step_by_step.title: Add one more filter before relying on it alone
step_by_step.detail: Pairing MACD divergence with RSI or a volume read (and never trading it against the dominant higher-timeframe trend) is what most of the sources behind this strategy point to as the difference between a clean signal and a false one.

videos.title: MACD Divergence Trading Strategy (Bullish, Bearish, Normal, Histogram and Line Divergence)
videos.note: Covers all four divergence variants (bullish/bearish, line/histogram) with chart examples of each, which is useful since MACD divergence shows up in more flavours than RSI divergence does.

strategies.name: Stochastic Oscillator Strategies
strategies.summary_one_line: Compares closing prices with recent ranges to flag stretched conditions.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how the Stochastic oscillator compares closing prices with recent ranges.
strategies.core_concept: The close's position within the N-period range (George Lane).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Slow Stochastic (14, 3, 3); 80/20 levels.

rules.entry: Buy a %K/%D cross up from below 20 in an uptrend (mirror for shorts).
rules.exit: At the opposing level.

market_conditions.struggles: Embedded readings (stuck above 80) in trends.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Counter-trend fading in a strong trend.

strategies.win_rate_note: A reversion profile: tends to win more often, with fatter occasional losses.

evidence.summary: Weak evidence overall.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Add the Stochastic with settings matched to your style
step_by_step.detail: The default is %K 14, %D 3. Faster settings (5,3,3) suit scalping, the default suits day trading, and slower settings (21,7,7) suit swing trading — the faster the setting, the more signals, but the more noise too.

step_by_step.title: Determine the underlying trend first
step_by_step.detail: Use a higher timeframe or a simple moving average (the 200 SMA is common) to establish whether the market is trending up, down, or range-bound, since that decides which Stochastic readings you'll actually act on.

step_by_step.title: Read the overbought/oversold zones in context
step_by_step.detail: Above 80 is overbought, below 20 is oversold — but in an uptrend, treat oversold readings as potential buying opportunities rather than automatic sell signals, and vice versa in a downtrend. Taking oversold as an automatic 'sell the top' signal against the trend is the most common misuse of this indicator.

step_by_step.title: Watch for the %K/%D crossover, not just the zone
step_by_step.detail: A %K line crossing above %D while both are below 20 suggests a possible bounce; %K crossing below %D while both are above 80 suggests a possible drop. The crossover is the actual trigger — being in the zone alone is not.

step_by_step.title: Add one layer of outside confirmation
step_by_step.detail: Use price action (a reversal candle), a nearby support/resistance level, or another indicator to support the Stochastic reading before acting on it. Stochastic alone, especially in a strong trend, tends to give crossovers well before the move is actually over.

step_by_step.title: Enter after the crossover and confirmation line up
step_by_step.detail: Place the entry once both the crossover and your chosen confirmation have happened, not on the crossover alone — this costs you a little in entry price but cuts out a large share of false signals.

step_by_step.title: Place a stop at the recent swing
step_by_step.detail: A stop just beyond the swing high or low that the setup formed against gives the trade room to be wrong without an arbitrarily tight exit.

step_by_step.title: Manage the trade to the opposing level or a fixed target
step_by_step.detail: Many traders exit (or trail) as Stochastic reaches the opposite extreme, or simply use a fixed risk-to-reward multiple if there's no clear nearby level to aim for.

videos.title: How Traders Really Use the Stochastic Oscillator (Beginner Guide + Real Examples)
videos.note: A beginner-pitched walkthrough of reading momentum, spotting reversals, timing pullbacks and confirming breakouts with the Stochastic — useful because it covers more than just the textbook overbought/oversold read.

strategies.name: CCI (Commodity Channel Index) Strategies
strategies.summary_one_line: Measures deviation from a typical price average for either momentum or reversion reads.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how the CCI measures deviation from a typical price average.
strategies.core_concept: Donald Lambert (1980). Typical price deviation, scaled by mean deviation.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: CCI(20); ±100 levels.

rules.entry: Trend entries: a cross above +100. Reversion: a cross back from ±100 extremes.
rules.exit: At the opposing level.

market_conditions.works_best: Depends on which of the two opposite uses is applied.
market_conditions.struggles: Confusing the trend and reversion interpretations.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Mixing the two uses in one system.

common_pitfalls: Mixing the trend and reversion interpretations.
strategies.win_rate_note: Depends on which variant (trend vs. reversion) is used.

evidence.summary: Weak evidence overall.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Add CCI to your chart
step_by_step.detail: Most platforms list it under 'Commodity Channel Index' in the indicators search. The default length is 20 periods.

step_by_step.title: Learn the key levels you're watching for
step_by_step.detail: CCI oscillates mostly between −100 and +100 in normal conditions; readings beyond ±200 are considered extreme. Your attention should mainly be on the 0, ±100 and ±200 lines.

step_by_step.title: Decide whether you're trading trend or reversion with it
step_by_step.detail: These are two different approaches with the same indicator, so pick one for a given setup rather than mixing signals from both at once.

step_by_step.title: For trend trading: wait for a zero-line break
step_by_step.detail: In a strong uptrend, treat a break above the zero line as a buy signal; in a downtrend, treat a break below zero as a sell signal. This is the slower, trend-following use of CCI.

step_by_step.title: For mean reversion: use the re-entry method
step_by_step.detail: Wait for CCI to drop below −100 (oversold), then wait for it to cross back above −100, and enter on the next candle. Mirror this for sells: wait for CCI above +100, then a cross back below it.

step_by_step.title: Filter with a longer-term moving average
step_by_step.detail: Only take buy signals when price is above a long-term moving average, and only take sell signals when price is below it — this keeps you from fading a strong trend with the reversion method.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop and target around the zero-line crossovers
step_by_step.detail: A short-term stop or target is often set at the next zero-line crossover; longer-term trades use the opposite extreme value as the target instead.

step_by_step.title: Treat every signal as conditional on the broader trend
step_by_step.detail: CCI readings mean very different things in a trending market versus a ranging one, so revisit step 3 each time before acting on a new signal.

videos.title: Master The CCI Indicator in 3 Minutes - Trading Made Simple!
videos.note: A quick, beginner-pitched run-through of what CCI measures and how to read zero-line crosses and trendline breaks — good as a first pass before the more advanced strategy videos out there.

strategies.name: Williams %R Strategies
strategies.summary_one_line: Locates the close within the recent high-low range to flag reversion points.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Williams %R locates the close within the recent high-low range.
strategies.core_concept: Larry Williams' inverted stochastic-type oscillator.

rules.entry: Buy on a reversal up from below −80 within an uptrend.
rules.exit: At the opposing level.

market_conditions.struggles: Embedded extremes in trends.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Redundant signals alongside Stochastic.

strategies.win_rate_note: A reversion profile, similar to Stochastic.

evidence.summary: Weak evidence overall.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Understand the inverted scale before anything else
step_by_step.detail: Unlike most oscillators, Williams %R reads from 0 (top) to −100 (bottom) — a reading near 0 is overbought and near −100 is oversold, which trips people up the first time they use it.

step_by_step.title: Pick a period length for your style
step_by_step.detail: 14 periods is the default, balancing speed and reliability. Use 7-10 for faster, noisier signals on quick swings, or 20-30 for smoother but slower signals.

step_by_step.title: Establish the broader trend direction
step_by_step.detail: Like the other oscillators here, Williams %R works best read with the trend rather than against it — confirm the direction on a higher timeframe or moving average first.

step_by_step.title: Watch for the indicator to leave the extreme and turn
step_by_step.detail: A common setup is buying once the indicator moves back above −80 after being below it (a reversal up from oversold), or selling once it moves back below −20 after being above it.

step_by_step.title: Confirm with a moving average before entering
step_by_step.detail: Wait for price to actually cross your chosen moving average in the signalled direction before entering, rather than acting the moment Williams %R ticks off its extreme.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the confirmed move and set a stop
step_by_step.detail: Place the stop beyond the recent swing high or low that the setup formed at.

step_by_step.title: Target major support/resistance or a fixed risk-to-reward
step_by_step.detail: Aim for the next clear support/resistance level, or simply use a 1:2 risk-to-reward ratio if no obvious level is nearby.

step_by_step.title: Re-check the trend before every new signal
step_by_step.detail: Because this is a bounded oscillator, it will keep producing overbought/oversold readings in a strong trend long before that trend actually ends — don't treat every reading as an entry.

videos.title: Williams R Indicator Explained For Beginners (Learn How To Use Williams R In Trading Strategy)
videos.note: A beginner-focused explanation of the indicator and how to build it into a basic strategy, which helps since Williams %R's inverted scale (0 to −100) is the first thing that trips people up.

strategies.name: Momentum / Rate of Change (ROC)
strategies.summary_one_line: Measures the speed of price movement over a set period.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how rate-of-change measures the speed of price movement over a set period.
strategies.core_concept: The percentage change over N periods. A positive reading means upward momentum.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: ROC(12) or ROC(125/250) for longer-term use.

rules.entry: Long when ROC crosses above zero (optionally with a filter).
rules.exit: Below zero.

asset_class_notes.futures: Core use case, a simple form of time-series momentum.

market_conditions.struggles: Sharp reversals.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Short lookbacks are noisy.

strategies.win_rate_note: A trend-following profile.

evidence.summary: Category evidence is strong for diversified futures (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012); single-market evidence is mixed.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Choose your look-back period
step_by_step.detail: 12 periods is the standard, balanced setting. Shorter (e.g. 6) reacts faster but whipsaws more; longer (e.g. 24) is smoother but slower to signal.

step_by_step.title: Add a trend filter alongside ROC
step_by_step.detail: ROC on its own just measures the percentage change over N periods — pair it with a simple moving average (a 20-period SMA is common) so you're only taking signals in the direction price is actually closing.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a zero-line crossover
step_by_step.detail: A move from negative to positive suggests upward momentum is building; from positive to negative suggests the opposite. The further ROC moves from zero, the stronger the momentum is read to be.

step_by_step.title: Confirm with your trend filter before acting
step_by_step.detail: Only take the bullish crossover when price is also closing above your moving average filter (and the mirror for bearish), to cut down on false signals in a choppy market.

step_by_step.title: Enter at the next candle open after confirmation
step_by_step.detail: Enter once both the ROC crossover and the trend filter line up, rather than acting mid-bar.

step_by_step.title: Place a stop just below (or above) the recent swing
step_by_step.detail: A stop at the recent swing low (longs) or swing high (shorts) gives the trade room while still capping the downside if the signal was wrong.

step_by_step.title: Watch for ROC to roll over as a trim signal
step_by_step.detail: When ROC peaks and turns back toward zero, it's often treated as a cue to trail the stop tighter or take partial profit, even before the zero-line cross happens.

step_by_step.title: Exit the remainder on the opposite zero-line cross
step_by_step.detail: Closing the rest of the position once ROC crosses back through zero keeps the exit rule as mechanical as the entry rule.

videos.title: How to Use the Rate of Change (ROC) Indicator: A Complete Trading Guide
videos.note: Frames ROC as a speedometer for price momentum and covers using it to spot trend exhaustion, which is the practical use case most traders get out of it beyond the basic zero-line cross.

strategies.name: Relative Strength / Cross-Sectional Momentum Rotation
strategies.summary_one_line: Ranks assets by recent performance to focus on relative leaders.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders rank assets by recent performance to focus on relative leaders.
strategies.core_concept: Assets that outperformed over the past 3–12 months have historically tended to keep outperforming in the short to medium term, per the academic momentum literature starting with Jegadeesh and Titman (1993). This is not the same as RSI.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Ratio charts, 6- or 12-month returns, ranking.

rules.entry: Hold the top-ranked assets and rebalance monthly.
rules.exit: When a holding falls out of the top group.
rules.stop: Position-level stops are less central than the rebalance rule itself.

asset_class_notes.stocks: Core use case: stocks, sector ETFs, country indices.
asset_class_notes.crypto: Rotation is popular but has a short history.

market_conditions.struggles: Sharp market rebounds, which can cause "momentum crashes".
market_conditions.failure_modes: Turnover costs eating into the edge.

strategies.win_rate_note: A moderate proportion of winners with known crash risk at turning points.

evidence.summary: Strong academic evidence for the factor before costs, with notable crash risk; retail implementation results are mixed.

strategies.platform_testability: Ranking needs a screener or external tools.

step_by_step.title: Pick your universe of assets
step_by_step.detail: The classic version uses the 11 S&P sector ETFs against the S&P 500 itself, but the same method works on any basket (country ETFs, asset classes, or a watchlist of individual stocks) as long as they're comparable.

step_by_step.title: Decide your look-back window
step_by_step.detail: 3-month and 6-month relative performance are the most commonly used windows in the research behind this strategy. Shorter windows react faster but rotate holdings more often; longer windows are steadier.

step_by_step.title: Calculate relative strength against the benchmark
step_by_step.detail: For each asset, compare its return over the look-back window to the benchmark's return over the same window — this is what separates genuine outperformance from an asset that's simply up because the whole market is up.

step_by_step.title: Rank every asset in your universe
step_by_step.detail: Order the whole basket from strongest relative performer to weakest. Some versions adjust each asset's return by its own volatility before ranking, so a steadier outperformer doesn't lose to a more volatile one.

step_by_step.title: Hold only the top-ranked group
step_by_step.detail: A common rule is holding the top 3-4 out of 11 sectors, or the top third of a larger universe, and avoiding (or shorting, in more advanced versions) the weakest group.

step_by_step.title: Set a fixed rebalance schedule
step_by_step.detail: Monthly rebalancing is the most common cadence in the research; some faster versions rebalance every 2-4 weeks. Pick one in advance and stick to it rather than reacting to short-term noise.

step_by_step.title: Exit a holding only when it drops out of the top group
step_by_step.detail: The exit rule is built into the rebalance itself — an asset leaves the portfolio once it's no longer ranked in your chosen top tier, not because of a price target or stop being hit.

step_by_step.title: Expect this to be a slower, lower-turnover approach
step_by_step.detail: This isn't a trade-by-trade setup like the other indicator strategies here — it's closer to a portfolio discipline, and it's judged over many rebalance cycles rather than individual trades.

videos.title: How to Find Sector Leadership with Relative Strength!
videos.note: A practical, retail-friendly take on using relative strength to identify leading sectors — less dense than the institutional Relative Rotation Graph (RRG) videos, which assume more charting background.

strategies.name: On-Balance Volume (OBV) Confirmation/Divergence
strategies.summary_one_line: Tracks cumulative volume flow alongside price to confirm or question a move.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how On-Balance Volume tracks cumulative volume flow alongside price.
strategies.core_concept: Joseph Granville. Volume is added on up days and subtracted on down days, so OBV trends may confirm or diverge from price.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: OBV, optionally with its own MA.

rules.entry: Confirm breakouts with an OBV breakout.
rules.exit: A divergence is treated as a warning to tighten up.

market_conditions.struggles: Single large-volume days distorting the read.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Treating OBV as a standalone signal.

common_pitfalls: Treating OBV as a standalone signal.
strategies.win_rate_note: No credible data on how often this wins exists.

evidence.summary: Weak. Lo and co-authors found volume added little to pattern information.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Add OBV below your price chart
step_by_step.detail: OBV has no inputs to set — it's a running total that adds the day's volume on an up day and subtracts it on a down day. What matters is its shape and direction, not its absolute number.

step_by_step.title: Use it to confirm breakouts first
step_by_step.detail: The simplest use: when price breaks a resistance level, check that OBV is also breaking its own recent high at the same time. If OBV confirms, the breakout has more volume support behind it; if it doesn't, treat the breakout with more caution.

step_by_step.title: Mark price's recent swing highs or lows for divergence
step_by_step.detail: For bearish divergence, watch for price printing a higher high. For bullish divergence, watch for price printing a lower low — same structure as RSI or MACD divergence, just measured against volume flow instead of momentum.

step_by_step.title: Compare that swing to OBV at the same points
step_by_step.detail: Bearish divergence: price makes a higher high while OBV makes a lower high (the rally isn't backed by equivalent buying volume). Bullish divergence: price makes a lower low while OBV makes a higher low.

step_by_step.title: Require at least two clear divergent swings
step_by_step.detail: A single mismatch between price and OBV is weak evidence on its own — look for the pattern to repeat across at least two swing points spanning several periods before treating it seriously.

step_by_step.title: Favour daily and weekly charts over intraday
step_by_step.detail: OBV divergence tends to be noticeably cleaner on daily and weekly charts; intraday volume is choppier and produces far more false divergences.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a price confirmation before entering
step_by_step.detail: For bullish divergence, wait for a bullish reversal candle or a break back above a recent high before entering. For bearish divergence, wait for a bearish engulfing candle or a breakdown of a recent low.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop beyond the recent swing and target the next level
step_by_step.detail: Stop just beyond the swing that formed the divergence, and target the prior support/resistance or a 1:2 risk-to-reward ratio if nothing else is close by.

videos.title: OBV Indicator Explained (On Balance Volume): Strategy + Divergence (TradingView)
videos.note: Covers OBV's best settings (there aren't many to set) alongside the divergence technique specifically, which is the part of OBV most worth learning well.

strategies.name: ADX/DMI Trend Strength
strategies.summary_one_line: Measures trend strength and direction using ADX and the directional indicators.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how ADX and the directional indicators measure trend strength and direction.
strategies.core_concept: Wilder (1978). +DI/−DI give direction, and ADX gives strength regardless of direction.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: ADX(14); threshold of about 20–25.

rules.entry: Trade +DI/−DI crosses only when ADX is above 25.
rules.exit: On the opposite DI cross or an ADX roll-over.

market_conditions.struggles: ADX lags and tends to peak near trend exhaustion.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Reading a rising ADX as bullish (it's direction-neutral).

common_pitfalls: Reading a rising ADX as bullish (it is direction-neutral).
strategies.win_rate_note: A trend-following profile.

evidence.summary: Weak/little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Add ADX/DMI with the standard 14-period setting
step_by_step.detail: This gives you three lines: +DI (upward movement strength), −DI (downward movement strength) and ADX itself (overall trend strength, regardless of direction).

step_by_step.title: Check ADX before anything else
step_by_step.detail: ADX above 25 suggests a trend is in place and worth trading with trend-following methods; below 20 suggests a weak trend or a range, where mean-reversion approaches tend to do better instead.

step_by_step.title: Watch for the +DI/−DI crossover for direction
step_by_step.detail: When +DI crosses above −DI, that's a buy signal; when +DI crosses below −DI, that's a sell signal — but only act on these once ADX confirms there's an actual trend to trade (step 2).

step_by_step.title: Apply the extreme point rule before entering
step_by_step.detail: On the day of a crossover, don't enter immediately. Note the day's high (for a buy signal) or low (for a sell signal) — that's the 'extreme point'. Only enter if price breaks that extreme on the next bar, which filters out a lot of crossovers that reverse immediately.

step_by_step.title: Read what ADX is doing, not just its level
step_by_step.detail: ADX crossing above 25 from below signals a trend starting; crossing below 25 from above signals it weakening back into consolidation; crossing above 40 signals a genuinely strong trend phase.

step_by_step.title: Scale your stop to the ADX reading
step_by_step.detail: Use a wider stop in strong-trend conditions (high ADX) since pullbacks tend to be deeper, and a tighter stop in weak-trend conditions (low ADX).

step_by_step.title: Exit on the opposite DI cross or an ADX roll-over
step_by_step.detail: Treat a −DI cross back above +DI (for a long) as your exit signal, or exit/tighten up when ADX itself starts falling from a high level, since that's telling you the trend is losing strength.

step_by_step.title: Add a multi-timeframe check for extra confidence
step_by_step.detail: Confirm the trend direction on a higher timeframe (daily or 4-hour) before taking entries on a lower one (1-hour or 15-minute) — trading only when both agree cuts down on a lot of false starts.

videos.title: The ADX Indicator Strategy (DMI) For Stock Beginners
videos.note: A beginner-focused walkthrough of setting up and reading ADX/DMI for finding and confirming trends, including platform setup on common charting tools.

strategies.name: Supertrend
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses an ATR-based band that flips above or below price to define a trailing trend line.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how the Supertrend indicator uses volatility to define a trailing trend line.
strategies.core_concept: An ATR-based band that flips above or below price (attributed to Olivier Seban).
strategies.tools_and_defaults: ATR period 10, multiplier 3 (TradingView default).

rules.entry: Long when price closes above the line (the line turns green).
rules.exit: The line flips.
rules.stop: The line itself, trailing with price.

market_conditions.struggles: Ranges, which cause whipsaws.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Optimising the multiplier to past data.

strategies.win_rate_note: A trend-following profile. Social media posts often show cherry-picked trending charts rather than a fair sample.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

image.caption: Synthetic price with an ATR-based Supertrend line flipping between support and resistance.

step_by_step.title: Choose settings matched to your trading style
step_by_step.detail: The default is period 10, multiplier 3. Scalpers often use period 7, multiplier 2 for faster signals; swing traders use period 14, multiplier 3-4 for fewer flips; volatile assets like crypto often use a multiplier of 5 to cut down on noise.

step_by_step.title: Watch the line's colour and position relative to price
step_by_step.detail: When the line sits below price and is green, that's a long bias. When it sits above price and is red, that's a short/exit bias — the line only ever sits on one side of price at a time.

step_by_step.title: Start by just observing before trading it
step_by_step.detail: Watch how the line behaves across both trending and sideways days on the exact instrument and timeframe you plan to trade, without risking anything — Supertrend whipsaws heavily in choppy, non-trending conditions.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the flip, in the new direction
step_by_step.detail: Go long when the line flips from red to green; go short (or exit an existing long) when it flips from green to red. This is the basic trend-following version of the strategy.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop at the Supertrend line itself
step_by_step.detail: The line value on your entry bar becomes your initial stop — this ties your risk directly to the indicator's own measure of volatility rather than an arbitrary distance.

step_by_step.title: Trail your stop as the trend continues
step_by_step.detail: Each new bar, move your stop to the current Supertrend line value. This lets you stay in a strong trend while still locking in progressively more protection as it extends.

step_by_step.title: Add a confirmation filter before trusting a flip
step_by_step.detail: A common combination is Supertrend plus a 14-period RSI: only take a long on a green flip if RSI is also above 50, confirming bullish momentum, and mirror this for shorts.

step_by_step.title: Backtest the exact flips on your instrument first
step_by_step.detail: Because Supertrend is purely reactive to price, how well it performs varies a lot by instrument and timeframe — check how it would have behaved recently before committing real risk to it.

videos.title: The Simplest SuperTrend Trading Strategy (Clear Entry & Exit Rules)
videos.note: A clean run-through of the basic flip-to-flip Supertrend approach with explicit entry and exit rules, good as a first pass before adding confirmation filters.

strategies.name: Parabolic SAR
strategies.summary_one_line: Trails price with an accelerating stop-and-reverse level.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Parabolic SAR trails price with an accelerating stop-and-reverse level.
strategies.core_concept: Wilder. The stop accelerates as the trend extends.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Step 0.02, maximum 0.2.

rules.entry: Always in the market, often filtered with ADX.
rules.exit: Reverse when price touches the SAR.

market_conditions.struggles: Constant reversals in ranges.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Using it without a trend filter.

common_pitfalls: Using it without a trend filter.
strategies.win_rate_note: A low proportion of winners in ranges, by design.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Set the standard acceleration parameters
step_by_step.detail: The reference configuration is a start of 0.02, an increment of 0.02, and a maximum of 0.20. Start sets the initial acceleration, increment controls how fast it speeds up after a new price extreme, and maximum caps it.

step_by_step.title: Understand this is a stop-and-reverse system by design
step_by_step.detail: Each entry signal is also the exit signal for the opposite position — when the dots flip, you exit entirely and (in the pure version) enter in the new direction, all in one action.

step_by_step.title: Wait for the candle to close before acting on a flip
step_by_step.detail: Act only after the candle closes below the dots (bearish flip) or above them (bullish flip) — reacting mid-bar to a flip that hasn't closed yet is a common source of false signals.

step_by_step.title: Enter at the next open or at the closing price
step_by_step.detail: Once a flip is confirmed by the close, enter a long position at the next market open (or with a limit order at the closing price of the flip bar).

step_by_step.title: Use the most recent SAR dot as your stop
step_by_step.detail: This gives you a built-in trailing stop — as the SAR dots update each new bar, your stop moves with them automatically.

step_by_step.title: Treat a flip against your position as your exit
step_by_step.detail: Monitor the dots every new candle. If they flip to the other side of price, that's your signal to exit (and, in the pure stop-and-reverse version, to flip direction).

step_by_step.title: Always pair SAR with a trend or momentum filter
step_by_step.detail: Parabolic SAR performs poorly in sideways markets, flipping back and forth repeatedly. Combining it with a 20-period EMA and a 14-period RSI, or only taking signals when ADX is above 25, filters out a large share of these false flips.

step_by_step.title: Exit the trade the moment PSAR flips, filter or no filter
step_by_step.detail: Whatever filter you use for entries, the exit rule stays mechanical: once the PSAR flips against your position, that's the exit, regardless of how the trade is doing.

videos.title: Parabolic SAR Indicator Explained For Beginners... Simple and Effective Exit Strategy
videos.note: Frames Parabolic SAR primarily as an exit/trailing-stop tool rather than a standalone entry signal, which matches how most experienced traders actually use it.

strategies.name: Heikin-Ashi Trend Trading
strategies.summary_one_line: Averages price data into modified candles to display trends more smoothly.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Heikin-Ashi candles average price data to display trends more smoothly.
strategies.core_concept: Modified candles: close = (O+H+L+C)/4, open = average of the prior HA open and close. Consecutive same-colour candles with no opposing wick suggest a strong trend.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: A built-in chart type on most platforms.

rules.entry: On a colour change with confirmation.
rules.exit: An opposing colour or doji-like candles.

market_conditions.struggles: Lag at turning points.
market_conditions.failure_modes: HA prices are not real traded prices, so a backtest filled at HA prices is unrealistic.

common_pitfalls: Backtesting fills on HA candles instead of real prices.
strategies.win_rate_note: HA-filled backtests can inflate the apparent proportion of winners — always re-test on standard candles before trusting a number like that.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: A built-in chart type; test on standard candles, not HA.

step_by_step.title: Switch your chart type to Heikin-Ashi
step_by_step.detail: Most platforms offer this as a chart-type toggle. Remember the candles are averaged (close = (O+H+L+C)/4) — they smooth out noise but no longer show the real open, high, low or close.

step_by_step.title: Start on a higher timeframe to read the overall trend
step_by_step.detail: Long runs of same-coloured candles usually indicate a strong trend; frequent colour alternation usually signals consolidation. If there's no clear run of one colour, it's generally better to wait rather than force a read.

step_by_step.title: Drop to your trading timeframe for confirmation
step_by_step.detail: Look for two or three consecutive candles in the same direction — ideally with little or no wick on the opposing side (little lower wick for bullish candles, little upper wick for bearish ones), which marks a genuinely strong move rather than a choppy one.

step_by_step.title: Treat wick-less candles as the strongest trend signal
step_by_step.detail: A long run of bullish candles with no lower wicks is read as a strong uptrend; a run of bearish candles with no upper wicks is read as a strong downtrend. Candles with wicks on both sides suggest the move is losing conviction.

step_by_step.title: Enter at the open of the next candle, using the real market price
step_by_step.detail: This is the step most people get wrong: enter using the actual market price, never the averaged Heikin-Ashi value, since the HA value isn't a real tradable price.

step_by_step.title: Switch back to a regular candlestick chart to set your stop
step_by_step.detail: Place the stop at the most recent swing high or low on the real price chart — not on the Heikin-Ashi candle's high or low, which is an average and not a real level the market actually touched.

step_by_step.title: Watch for a colour change or shrinking bodies as an exit cue
step_by_step.detail: A colour flip, or a run of small-bodied candles with wicks on both sides, is typically read as the trend losing steam — that's the point to tighten up or exit rather than wait for a full reversal.

step_by_step.title: Don't act on the first colour change without confirmation
step_by_step.detail: A single flipped candle or doji-like bar can be noise rather than a genuine reversal — wait for the next candle, or support from another indicator, before treating it as confirmed.

videos.title: How to Trade Heikin Ashi Candlesticks l Step by Step Beginner's Guide
videos.note: A beginner-pitched, step-by-step walkthrough of reading Heikin-Ashi candles for trend strength, which is the main practical use case for this chart type.

strategies.name: ATR Volatility Breakout and ATR-Based Stops
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses Average True Range to size stops and define volatility-based breakouts.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Average True Range is used to size stops and define volatility-based breakouts.
strategies.core_concept: ATR (Wilder) measures typical range. Breakouts of more than k×ATR from a reference (the prior close or open) signal expansion. ATR stops adapt to volatility; Chandelier exits trail by 3×ATR from the highest high.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: ATR(14), multiples of 1.5–3.

rules.entry: Price exceeds the open plus k×ATR.
rules.exit: A Chandelier-style trailing exit.

market_conditions.struggles: False expansions.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Assuming a stop guarantees the exit price (slippage and gaps).

common_pitfalls: Assuming a stop guarantees the fill price.
strategies.win_rate_note: A breakout-style profile.

evidence.summary: ATR sizing is integral to the documented trend systems; standalone breakouts have mixed evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.
sources: StockCharts ChartSchool, "Average True Range" and "Chandelier Exit"

step_by_step.title: Add ATR with its standard 14-period setting
step_by_step.detail: ATR measures the average size of a bar's trading range over the chosen period — it doesn't tell you direction, only how much an instrument is typically moving.

step_by_step.title: Identify a consolidation phase first
step_by_step.detail: Look for price trading within a narrow range, with ATR itself relatively low and flat — this is the 'coiled spring' condition the breakout strategy is designed to catch the release from.

step_by_step.title: Watch for ATR to start rising
step_by_step.detail: A meaningful increase in ATR signals that volatility is expanding, which is what you want to see alongside a price move out of the range, not a move on flat or falling volatility.

step_by_step.title: Define your breakout trigger as a multiple of ATR
step_by_step.detail: A common rule is entering when price closes beyond the day's open (or the prior close) by more than k times ATR — using ATR instead of a fixed point/pip distance means the trigger automatically adapts to how volatile the instrument currently is.

step_by_step.title: Enter in the direction of the confirmed breakout
step_by_step.detail: Enter once price has closed beyond the ATR-based trigger level, in the direction of the move — this dynamic threshold is specifically meant to filter out minor price wiggles that aren't a genuine expansion.

step_by_step.title: Set your initial stop as a different ATR multiple
step_by_step.detail: A separate, usually smaller multiple of ATR from your entry (entry minus m×ATR for longs) gives you a stop sized to current volatility rather than an arbitrary fixed amount.

step_by_step.title: Trail the stop with a Chandelier-style exit as the trade runs
step_by_step.detail: The Chandelier Exit trails the stop from the highest high reached since entry, minus a multiple of ATR (and the mirror for shorts) — this lets the stop follow the trade without giving back the whole move on a pullback.

step_by_step.title: Reassess if volatility collapses again
step_by_step.detail: If ATR falls back toward its pre-breakout level, the expansion that triggered the trade may be over — treat that as a cue to tighten the stop further rather than assuming the move will keep going.

videos.title: How To Use ATR For Stop Loss In Trading
videos.note: Focuses specifically on using ATR to size stops to current volatility rather than a fixed distance, which is the part of this strategy most traders get the most direct use out of.

strategies.name: Keltner Channel Trend/Pullback
strategies.summary_one_line: Frames price around an average using ATR-based bands for trend and pullback reads.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how Keltner Channels frame price around an average using ATR-based bands.
strategies.core_concept: An EMA plus or minus an ATR multiple. Closes outside the band show trend strength, and pullbacks to the EMA are entries.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: EMA 20, ATR 10, ×2 (StockCharts default).

rules.entry: In an uptrend (closes above the upper band), buy a pullback to the middle EMA.
rules.exit: At the opposing band.

market_conditions.struggles: Ranges.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Confusing it with Bollinger behaviour.

strategies.win_rate_note: A trend-following profile.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Add Keltner Channels with the standard setup
step_by_step.detail: A 20-period EMA as the middle line, with the upper and lower bands set at an ATR multiple above and below it (common multiples are 1.5-2x ATR).

step_by_step.title: Establish the channel's slope and direction
step_by_step.detail: An upward-sloping channel with a pattern of higher highs and higher lows defines an uptrend setup; a downward-sloping channel with lower highs and lower lows defines a downtrend setup.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a pullback toward the middle line
step_by_step.detail: In an uptrend, wait for price to pull back from the upper band toward the centreline EMA (or into the lower half of the channel) rather than chasing price while it's still extended at the upper band.

step_by_step.title: Check that the prior swing low hasn't broken
step_by_step.detail: The pullback should hold above the previous swing low — if that level breaks during the pullback, the trend structure itself is now in question, and this setup no longer applies.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a clear bullish (or bearish) trigger at the centreline
step_by_step.detail: Don't enter on the pullback alone — wait for a specific trigger such as a bullish engulfing candle at the centreline, a reclaim of a short-term high, or a break of the pullback's own minor trendline.

step_by_step.title: Enter on the trigger, with the trend
step_by_step.detail: For the mirror short setup: a downward-sloping channel, a pullback up into the upper half, and a bearish trigger at the centreline.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop beyond the pullback's swing
step_by_step.detail: Stop just past the pullback's low (longs) or high (shorts) — ideally not sitting exactly on a channel line, since price can briefly tag a band without the setup actually failing.

step_by_step.title: Target the opposite band
step_by_step.detail: The far channel line (upper band for longs, lower band for shorts) is the typical target, which tends to give roughly a 2:1 reward-to-risk ratio since the stop distance is usually about half the distance to that target.

videos.title: Keltner Channel Trading Strategy Explained For Beginners
videos.note: A beginner-focused explanation of how to use Keltner Channels for trend and pullback trading, useful background before the more advanced backtested versions out there.

strategies.name: Moving-Average Pullback (Trend Continuation)
strategies.summary_one_line: Waits for pullbacks to a moving average within an established trend.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders wait for pullbacks to a moving average within an established trend.
strategies.core_concept: In trends, retracements to a dynamic average (e.g. the 20 or 50 EMA) offer defined-risk continuation entries.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: 20/50 EMA plus a trend filter (200 SMA).

rules.entry: With price above a rising 50 EMA, buy a bullish reversal bar at the 20 EMA.
rules.exit: At the next resistance or a trailing stop.

market_conditions.struggles: Pullbacks that become full reversals.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Buying every touch of the average regardless of context.

strategies.win_rate_note: A moderate profile; no specific rule has been independently tested.

evidence.summary: Category trend evidence only; this specific rule is weakly evidenced.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Confirm the trend with two moving averages
step_by_step.detail: A common setup uses the 20 EMA and 50 EMA: the 20 EMA staying above the 50 EMA signals an ongoing uptrend, and the 20 EMA below the 50 EMA signals a downtrend.

step_by_step.title: Be patient and wait for the pullback to actually happen
step_by_step.detail: Once the trend is established, wait for price to retrace back to a key moving average (the 20 or 50 EMA) rather than chasing it while it's still extended — pullbacks typically retrace somewhere between 20-62% of the preceding move, often near the 38.2%, 50% or 61.8% Fibonacci levels too.

step_by_step.title: Watch which moving average price is pulling back to
step_by_step.detail: A shallower pullback that holds the 20 EMA suggests a stronger trend; a deeper one that reaches the 50 EMA is still valid but suggests the trend has lost a bit more steam.

step_by_step.title: Look for a specific confirmation candle
step_by_step.detail: A bullish engulfing candle or a hammer at the moving average, in an uptrend, both suggest buyers are stepping back in. The mirror patterns — a bearish engulfing candle or a shooting star — suggest the same for a downtrend.

step_by_step.title: Enter once the confirmation candle closes
step_by_step.detail: Enter as price shows signs of resuming the trend, rather than anticipating the bounce before it's actually confirmed.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop beyond the pullback's extreme
step_by_step.detail: Stop slightly below the recent swing low (uptrend) or above the recent swing high (downtrend) that the pullback formed.

step_by_step.title: Target the previous high, a resistance level, or a fixed ratio
step_by_step.detail: Common targets are the prior swing high (for longs), a known resistance level, or simply a 1:2 risk-to-reward ratio from your stop distance.

step_by_step.title: Reset and wait for the next pullback once the trade closes
step_by_step.detail: This is a repeatable, trend-following setup rather than a one-off trade — in a persistent trend, the same process can be applied again at the next pullback to the moving average.

videos.title: Trade Pullbacks Like a Pro: Simple Moving Average Strategy That Works
videos.note: Covers the moving-average pullback approach alongside basic trend trading and multi-timeframe context, which is useful since this setup depends heavily on correctly reading the higher-timeframe trend first.

strategies.name: Pivot Points
strategies.summary_one_line: Calculates reference support/resistance levels from the prior session using floor-trader formulas.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how floor-trader pivot points calculate reference levels from the prior session.
strategies.core_concept: Standard formulas: P = (H+L+C)/3, R1 = 2P−L, S1 = 2P−H, R2 = P+(H−L), S2 = P−(H−L). Fibonacci, Camarilla and Woodie variants exist.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Daily pivots for intraday; weekly pivots for swing.

rules.entry: Fade S1/R1 in ranges; trade breaks of R1/S1 in trends.
rules.exit: P is the bias line; the next pivot level is the target.

asset_class_notes.forex: Depends on the chosen session close (commonly New York, 5pm ET).
asset_class_notes.crypto: The UTC daily close is arbitrary.

market_conditions.struggles: Trend days, which blow through levels.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Inconsistent session settings across instruments.

strategies.win_rate_note: Fade versions have a reversion-style profile.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Calculate the standard pivot and its levels
step_by_step.detail: P = (H+L+C)/3 using the prior period's high, low and close. From there: R1 = 2P−L, S1 = 2P−H, R2 = P+(H−L), S2 = P−(H−L), with R3 and S3 extending the pattern further. Most charting platforms calculate and plot these automatically.

step_by_step.title: Use the central pivot (P) as your daily bias line
step_by_step.detail: Price trading above P for the session is generally read as a bullish bias for the day; trading below P is read as bearish — this is the first, simplest read before looking at any of the other levels.

step_by_step.title: Decide whether the market is trending or ranging
step_by_step.detail: This decision changes how you use every level below it — pivot points are best used for trend breakouts in a trending market, and best avoided (or used only for the bounce strategy) in a ranging one.

step_by_step.title: In ranging conditions, trade the bounce off S1/R1
step_by_step.detail: Wait for price to reach S1 or R1, then look for a bullish (at S1) or bearish (at R1) candlestick pattern, or another indicator turning in your favour, before entering — don't fade the level purely because price touched it.

step_by_step.title: In trending conditions, trade the breakout of R1/S1
step_by_step.detail: In a strong uptrend, enter aggressively as price breaks decisively above R1 or R2, or wait for a retest where the broken resistance now holds as support before entering with more confirmation.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop just below the support (bounce) or the breakout level (trend)
step_by_step.detail: For a bounce trade, stop just below the support level; for a breakout trade, stop just below the level that was broken, since a failed retest there invalidates the setup.

step_by_step.title: Target the next pivot level
step_by_step.detail: R1/R2 (or S1/S2 for shorts) are the typical targets — the central pivot (P) itself is treated as bias, not usually a target.

step_by_step.title: Re-calculate at the start of each new session
step_by_step.detail: Daily pivots use the prior day's high/low/close, weekly pivots use the prior week's, and so on — recalculate fresh levels at the start of each period you trade rather than carrying old ones forward.

videos.title: Pivot Points Day Trading Strategy That Actually Works!
videos.note: A practical day-trading walkthrough of using pivot levels, which pairs well with the bounce-versus-breakout distinction that's the most important judgment call in this strategy.

strategies.name: VWAP Reversion and VWAP Trend
strategies.summary_one_line: Uses the session VWAP as a reference for intraday fair value, fading extremes or following pullbacks.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how intraday traders use the session VWAP as a reference for fair value and trend.
strategies.core_concept: The session VWAP is the volume-weighted average price. Institutions use it as an execution benchmark. Price above a rising VWAP suggests buyers are in control. Extremes at 2–3 standard-deviation bands may revert.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Session VWAP with standard-deviation bands.

rules.entry: Trend: buy the first pullback to VWAP in a strong open. Reversion: fade a band-extreme back to VWAP.
rules.exit: VWAP itself (reversion) or a trailing stop (trend).
rules.stop: Below VWAP (trend) or beyond the band (reversion).

asset_class_notes.forex: Uses tick volume as a proxy.

market_conditions.works_best: Depends on which use: trend days favour the trend variant, balanced days favour reversion.
market_conditions.struggles: Trend days defeat reversion; chop around VWAP defeats the trend variant.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Using VWAP on multi-day charts without anchoring it properly.

common_pitfalls: Using VWAP on multi-day charts without anchoring.
strategies.win_rate_note: No credible independent data exists on how often either variant wins.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Built into TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Anchor VWAP to the session open
step_by_step.detail: For intraday trading, VWAP should reset at the start of each session so it reflects that day's volume-weighted fair value, not a running average carried over from previous days.

step_by_step.title: Plot standard-deviation bands around VWAP
step_by_step.detail: Bands at one and two (sometimes three) standard deviations above and below VWAP expand and contract with volatility, and are what the reversion side of this strategy actually trades off of.

step_by_step.title: Read the day's regime before picking an approach
step_by_step.detail: Watch whether a push away from VWAP gets strong follow-through (suggesting a trending session, favouring trend trades with VWAP) or gets rejected back toward VWAP (suggesting a sideways session, favouring reversion trades).

step_by_step.title: For reversion: wait for price to reach an extreme band
step_by_step.detail: Price needs to trade to or beyond the second standard-deviation band, during sideways/choppy conditions with no strong news driver, before the reversion setup applies at all.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a rejection candle at that extreme before entering
step_by_step.detail: A long upper wick at the upper band, or a long lower wick at the lower band, signals that buyers or sellers absorbed the push — that rejection candle, not the band touch itself, is the actual entry trigger.

step_by_step.title: For trend trades: buy pullbacks to VWAP instead of fading it
step_by_step.detail: On a day that's showing strong directional follow-through, treat the first pullback to VWAP as a continuation entry in the direction of that follow-through, rather than fading the move.

step_by_step.title: Set your target and stop around VWAP itself
step_by_step.detail: For reversion trades, a first target is the midpoint back toward VWAP (around 1 to 1.5R), with a stop placed just beyond the 2SD band; if price pushes through to the 3SD band, the reversion read is broken and it's time to exit. For trend trades, VWAP itself often becomes the trailing stop level.

step_by_step.title: Avoid this strategy entirely on strong trend days
step_by_step.detail: VWAP reversion performs badly on days with a clear, strong trend and no chop — a regime filter (step 3) isn't optional, it's what keeps this strategy from losing badly on the wrong kind of day.

videos.title: VWAP Trading Strategy Explained (Best Entry & Exit Setup)
videos.note: Covers both entry and exit mechanics around VWAP specifically, which matters here since knowing when to exit a reversion trade (back at VWAP, or at the first standard-deviation band) is as important as the entry.

strategies.name: Opening Range Breakout (ORB)
strategies.summary_one_line: Defines the first minutes of a session and plans around moves beyond that range.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders define the first minutes of a session and plan around moves beyond that range.
strategies.core_concept: Associated with Toby Crabel's work (1990). The first 5–60 minutes set the day's initial balance, and a break may indicate the day's direction.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: First 5, 15 or 30 minutes' high/low; ATR; relative volume.

rules.entry: A break of the opening-range high.
rules.exit: At the close or a measured target.
rules.stop: At the opening-range low (or a fraction of ATR).

asset_class_notes.forex: The London/New York opens substitute for a defined open.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy days, where false breakouts dominate.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Ignoring slippage and costs right at the open.

strategies.win_rate_note: A low-proportion-of-winners, larger-average-winner profile in the versions that have been tested.

evidence.summary: Zarattini and Aziz (2023, SSRN) and Zarattini, Barbon and Aziz (2024, SSRN) report strong backtests for a 5-minute ORB on the top-20 "Stocks in Play" by relative volume, 2016–2023. Caveats: not peer-reviewed; co-author Andrew Aziz runs a trading-education business (a commercial conflict); a plain ORB without stock selection was reportedly weak — selection did most of the work; commentators note slippage and commissions may matter greatly.

strategies.platform_testability: Feasible in Pine Script.
strategies.data_requirement: Intraday data and a scanner for relative volume.
sources: Crabel, "Day Trading with Short Term Price Patterns and Opening Range Breakout"

image.caption: A fabricated opening range with price breaking above it later in the session.

step_by_step.title: Pick your opening-range window
step_by_step.detail: 5, 15 or 30 minutes after the open are the most common choices — a 15-minute window is the most widely used, balancing speed of signal against reliability.

step_by_step.title: Draw the range's high and low
step_by_step.detail: On a 1-, 3- or 5-minute chart, mark the highest high and lowest low of that opening window as a box — that box is the 'opening range' the rest of the strategy is built around.

step_by_step.title: Favour instruments with a reason to move
step_by_step.detail: This strategy works best on stocks or instruments with high trading volume, pre-market news, an earnings announcement, a gap at the open, or otherwise unusual momentum — a quiet, low-volume name is a weak candidate for it.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a candle close beyond the range, not just a wick
step_by_step.detail: A bullish breakout needs a candle to close above the range high; a bearish breakout needs a close below the range low. A wick alone that pokes outside the range and closes back inside is not a confirmed breakout.

step_by_step.title: Check volume on the breakout candle
step_by_step.detail: Relative volume (RVOL) above about 1.5, with the breakout candle's volume higher than the prior 5-10 bars, meaningfully increases the odds the breakout holds rather than immediately failing.

step_by_step.title: Choose between an aggressive or a retest entry
step_by_step.detail: An aggressive entry takes the breakout as soon as it's confirmed; a more conservative entry waits for price to pull back and retest the broken level before entering, trading a worse average price for better confirmation.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop at the opposite side of the range
step_by_step.detail: For a long entered on an upside breakout, stop below the range low; for a short, stop above the range high.

step_by_step.title: Target a multiple of the range itself
step_by_step.detail: A first target of 1x the range's height is common, with further targets at 2x the range or at the next session level (such as the pre-market high/low or VWAP), aiming for at least a 1:1 risk-to-reward and often 1.5-2:1 when conditions are strong.

videos.title: MASTER the 15-Minute ORB in 8 Minutes [Opening Range Breakout]
videos.note: A condensed walkthrough of the 15-minute opening-range version specifically, which is the most commonly used window for this strategy.

strategies.name: Gap Fill and Gap-and-Go
strategies.summary_one_line: Two opposite approaches to price gaps at the open: fading small gaps back, or following large catalyst-driven gaps.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the two opposite ways traders approach price gaps at the open.
strategies.core_concept: "Gap fill" assumes small, news-light gaps tend to retrace toward the prior close. "Gap-and-go" assumes large, catalyst-driven gaps on high volume continue.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Pre-market and opening-range levels.

rules.entry: Fill: fade the gap. Go: buy a break of the pre-market or opening high.
rules.exit: The prior close (fill) or a trailing target (go).
rules.stop: Beyond the opening extreme (fill) or below the opening range (go).

asset_class_notes.stocks: Core use case, especially around earnings.
asset_class_notes.forex: Gaps occur mainly at the weekend open.
asset_class_notes.crypto: No session gaps except on CME futures.

market_conditions.works_best: Matching the gap type to the right variant (news-light vs. catalyst-driven).
market_conditions.struggles: Using the wrong variant for the gap type.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Ignoring the catalyst and float.

strategies.win_rate_note: "Gaps always fill" is a misleading claim to avoid repeating.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Needs extended-hours data.

step_by_step.title: Identify the gap at the open
step_by_step.detail: A gap occurs when price opens meaningfully above or below the previous day's close — note the size of the gap (often expressed as a percentage) as your first filter.

step_by_step.title: Check for a catalyst behind the gap
step_by_step.detail: A strong catalyst (an earnings beat, FDA approval, M&A news) reduces the odds of the gap filling and favours the gap-and-go approach. No catalyst, or a weak one (an analyst note, sector sympathy), favours the gap-fill approach instead.

step_by_step.title: Check pre-market and early volume
step_by_step.detail: High pre-market volume on the gap suggests genuine institutional interest rather than a handful of retail orders moving a thin stock — low volume on a big gap is a warning sign either way.

step_by_step.title: Let the first few minutes of chaos settle
step_by_step.detail: For a potential gap-fill trade, watch the first 15 minutes: if the stock fails to make a new high (on a gap-up) and shows rejection candles, the odds of a fill increase. For a potential gap-and-go trade, let the first 5-minute candle close before acting at all.

step_by_step.title: For gap-and-go: enter above the early high with volume behind it
step_by_step.detail: Enter above the high of the first few minutes once that first candle closes, with the stop placed below the low of the same window — this is a continuation trade, riding the gap's direction.

step_by_step.title: For gap-fill: enter on a break of the opening range, against the gap
step_by_step.detail: Enter when price breaks below the opening range (for a gap-up fill trade), with the stop placed above the high of day — this is a reversion trade, betting the gap closes back toward the prior close.

step_by_step.title: Target appropriately for each approach
step_by_step.detail: For gap-and-go, trail the stop behind each new opening-range retest rather than exiting the whole position at once. For gap-fill, target the previous close — the actual 'fill' level — and consider taking partial profit at the halfway point.

step_by_step.title: Never run both approaches on the same gap at once
step_by_step.detail: Gap-fill and gap-and-go are opposite bets on the same setup — decide which one the catalyst and early price action supports (steps 2-4) before choosing a side, rather than trying to play both.

videos.title: This Gap Trading Strategy Prints You Money (Gap Up, Gap Down, Gap Fill)
videos.note: Covers gap-up, gap-down and gap-fill scenarios in one video, which suits this strategy since it's really two opposite approaches (continuation vs. reversion) to the same setup.

strategies.name: Inside Bar / NR7 Volatility Contraction
strategies.summary_one_line: Marks narrow-range and inside bars as volatility contraction before expansion.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how narrow-range and inside bars are used to mark volatility contraction.
strategies.core_concept: Crabel's NR4/NR7 (the narrowest range in 4 or 7 bars) and inside bars mark compression before expansion.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: NR4/NR7 range scans, or a simple inside-bar check.

rules.entry: A buy-stop above and a sell-stop below the bar, cancelling the other once one triggers.
rules.exit: At a measured target.
rules.stop: At the opposite side of the bar.

market_conditions.works_best: Compression ahead of a real move.
market_conditions.struggles: Double-sided whipsaws.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Ignoring the broader trend context.

strategies.win_rate_note: A breakout-style profile.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Easy to code.

step_by_step.title: Understand what you're screening for
step_by_step.detail: An inside bar has its full range contained within the prior bar's range. NR7 is a bar whose range is the smallest of the last 7 bars (including itself). Both describe the same underlying idea: volatility has contracted.

step_by_step.title: Build a watchlist using either (or both) conditions
step_by_step.detail: Scan for instruments currently printing an NR7 bar, an inside bar, or the stricter combination of both (sometimes called ID/NR4 when paired with a 4-bar range check) — most charting platforms can screen for these automatically.

step_by_step.title: Treat the pattern as a volatility-contraction signal, not a direction signal
step_by_step.detail: The idea mirrors a Bollinger Band squeeze: a period of unusually low volatility tends to be followed by a period of higher volatility — the pattern doesn't tell you which way the expansion will break, only that one is more likely coming.

step_by_step.title: Mark the narrow bar's high and low as your trigger levels
step_by_step.detail: These two levels — the top and bottom of the contracted bar — become the breakout triggers for whichever direction the market actually chooses.

step_by_step.title: Place entry stops on both sides
step_by_step.detail: A buy-stop just above the narrow bar's high and a sell-stop just below its low, with one order automatically cancelling the other once either is triggered — this is a 'straddle' approach that doesn't require you to predict direction in advance.

step_by_step.title: Let whichever side triggers first become your position
step_by_step.detail: Once price breaks one side, you're in that direction, and the untouched opposite-side order is cancelled.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop at the opposite side of the narrow bar
step_by_step.detail: If you're long after an upside break, your stop sits at the low of the narrow bar (now acting as the opposite stop-and-reverse point); mirror this for a short entry.

step_by_step.title: Target a measured move from the breakout
step_by_step.detail: A common approach projects the height of the narrow bar's range (or a recent average range) from the breakout point as a first target, adjusting based on how strongly the move is following through.
