strategies.name: Dow Theory
strategies.summary_one_line: Century-old principles that define trends by sequences of highs and lows.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the century-old principles that define trends by sequences of highs and lows.
strategies.core_concept: From Charles Dow and later Hamilton and Rhea: markets have three trends (primary, secondary, minor); primary trends have three phases; averages must confirm each other; volume confirms the trend; a trend persists until a definitive reversal.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price only.

rules.entry: An uptrend means higher highs and higher lows; enter in the direction of the confirmed trend.
rules.exit: A reversal is confirmed when a lower high is followed by a break of the prior low.
rules.stop: Below the most recent confirmed higher low.

asset_class_notes.forex: The higher-high/higher-low logic applies the same way.
asset_class_notes.crypto: The higher-high/higher-low logic applies the same way.
asset_class_notes.futures: The higher-high/higher-low logic applies the same way.

market_conditions.struggles: Choppy markets, where confirmation is slow.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Late signals relative to the actual turn.

common_pitfalls: Rigid confirmation demands that arrive very late.
strategies.win_rate_note: A trend-following profile.

evidence.summary: Historical studies are mixed and older.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual chart reading.

step_by_step.title: Learn the three trend timeframes
step_by_step.detail: Dow Theory separates the primary trend (the broad, months-to-years direction), the secondary trend (weeks-to-months corrections against it) and the minor trend (day-to-day noise). Use a weekly chart for the primary trend, daily for secondary, and intraday only for the minor trend.

step_by_step.title: Confirm the primary trend with higher highs and higher lows
step_by_step.detail: An uptrend is defined by a consistent pattern of higher highs and higher lows; a downtrend by lower highs and lower lows. This structural read is the foundation everything else in the theory builds on.

step_by_step.title: Look for confirmation across related indices
step_by_step.detail: The classic version of this requires the Dow Jones Industrial Average and Dow Jones Transportation Average to move in the same direction before a trend is considered valid — the modern equivalent is checking that a market's major index and a closely related gauge (for example, a sector index and its leading component) are telling the same story.

step_by_step.title: Check that volume supports the trend
step_by_step.detail: Rising prices on increasing volume is read as a strong, healthy trend. Look for above-average volume on moves with the trend and lower volume on counter-trend pullbacks.

step_by_step.title: Expect and wait out secondary reactions
step_by_step.detail: A primary trend doesn't move in a straight line — secondary reactions typically retrace 33-66% of the move so far. Don't treat a pullback of this size as a trend change; wait for it to end and for price to resume with volume support before acting.

step_by_step.title: Only trade in the direction of the confirmed primary trend
step_by_step.detail: Enter in the direction of the established higher-high/higher-low (or lower-high/lower-low) structure, once a secondary reaction has run its course — Dow Theory is a trend-following framework, not a reversal-picking one.

step_by_step.title: Treat a reversal as unconfirmed until proven
step_by_step.detail: A trend is assumed intact until it gives a clear signal otherwise — specifically, a lower high followed by a break of the prior swing low (for an uptrend) is what marks a confirmed reversal, not a single lower high on its own.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop below the most recent confirmed higher low
step_by_step.detail: This keeps your risk tied to the same structural logic the strategy uses to define the trend in the first place, and apply 1-2% account risk per trade as a general rule, reducing it further during high-volatility periods like earnings season.

videos.title: Master Dow Theory: Read Market Trends Like a Professional Trader
videos.note: Frames Dow Theory as a structured way to read overall market direction rather than reacting to every short-term wiggle, which is how it's actually used by most traders today.

strategies.name: Supply and Demand Zones
strategies.summary_one_line: Marks areas where price left sharply as possible zones of unfilled orders.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders mark areas where price left sharply as possible zones of unfilled orders.
strategies.core_concept: Zones are "base" candles before strong departures (rally-base-rally, drop-base-drop and similar). They assume unfilled institutional orders remain there, an idea close to the ICT order block.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Manual zone marking on a price chart.

rules.entry: At the first return to a "fresh" zone.
rules.exit: The opposing zone.

market_conditions.struggles: Zones that break on a second or third test.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Subjective zone width leading to inconsistent results.

strategies.win_rate_note: Often marketed with high reward-to-risk screenshots implying a strong edge. Treat that framing with caution.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual drawing on TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Find a clear, sharp move away from a level
step_by_step.detail: Look for a rally or decline that departed quickly and decisively from a price area — the sharper and faster the departure, the more significant the zone it left behind is considered.

step_by_step.title: Trace the move back to where it started
step_by_step.detail: Follow the rally or decline backward to its origin — the small area of consolidation just before the sharp move began is the 'base', and that base is what becomes your zone.

step_by_step.title: Mark the zone as a range, not a single line
step_by_step.detail: Draw a rectangle encompassing the full price range of that base/consolidation area, rather than a single horizontal line — zones are areas where orders are thought to sit, not an exact price point.

step_by_step.title: Check volume at the base for extra confidence
step_by_step.detail: Higher volume during the base's formation is read as stronger evidence of real demand (or supply) sitting in that area, versus a quiet, low-volume base.

step_by_step.title: Prefer zones price hasn't returned to yet
step_by_step.detail: A 'fresh' zone — one price hasn't revisited since it was formed — is considered to have a better chance of producing a reaction than one that's already been tested and partly used up.

step_by_step.title: Confirm the zone across two timeframes if you can
step_by_step.detail: Identify the zone on a higher timeframe (e.g. daily) first, then zoom into a lower timeframe (e.g. 4-hour) to find a smaller zone that sits within it — when both line up, the case for a reaction there is considered stronger.

step_by_step.title: Wait for price to return and show a reaction, not just arrive
step_by_step.detail: For a demand zone, wait for a bounce to actually show up — a bullish engulfing candle or a visible surge in buying — rather than entering the instant price touches the zone. Mirror this for supply zones and bearish rejection.

step_by_step.title: Set your stop just beyond the zone and target the opposite one
step_by_step.detail: A stop a little below a demand zone (or above a supply zone) gives the trade room without being unreasonably wide, and the next opposing zone (supply for a long, demand for a short) becomes the typical target.

videos.note: A step-by-step beginner's guide to marking and trading supply/demand zones, applicable to both forex and stocks, which matches how this strategy is used across different markets.

strategies.name: Head and Shoulders (and Inverse)
strategies.summary_one_line: Three peaks with the middle one highest; a break of the neckline suggests a trend reversal.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the head-and-shoulders reversal pattern and how its neckline and measured move are defined.
strategies.core_concept: Three peaks with the middle one highest. A break of the neckline suggests a trend reversal. Lo, Mamaysky and Wang defined it formally from five consecutive extrema.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price chart, optional volume confirmation.

rules.entry: Short on a close below the neckline (or on a retest).
rules.exit: The head-to-neckline height projected down.

asset_class_notes.forex: Osler and Chang (1995) tested it in currencies, with results varying by currency.

market_conditions.works_best: A genuine topping or bottoming process.
market_conditions.struggles: Necklines that break and then reverse back.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Labelling unfinished patterns before confirmation.

strategies.win_rate_note: Published success rates for this pattern are unverified.

evidence.summary: Lo and co-authors found incremental information; FX evidence varies by currency.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual or auto-pattern tools on TradingView.

image.caption: A schematic head-and-shoulders top with its neckline marked.

step_by_step.title: Identify the three peaks (or troughs for the inverse)
step_by_step.detail: Classic head and shoulders: a left shoulder, a higher middle peak (the head), then a right shoulder roughly matching the left — all forming after an uptrend. Inverse head and shoulders is the same shape flipped upside down, forming after a downtrend, with three troughs instead of three peaks.

step_by_step.title: Draw the neckline
step_by_step.detail: Connect the two low points between the shoulders and the head (for the standard pattern), or the two high points between them (for the inverse) — this line is what the pattern needs to break for confirmation.

step_by_step.title: Wait for a decisive close beyond the neckline
step_by_step.detail: Confirmation happens when price closes clearly beyond the neckline, ideally on strong volume — a brief wick through the neckline that closes back on the other side doesn't count as confirmation.

step_by_step.title: Choose between an immediate entry or a retest entry
step_by_step.detail: You can enter as soon as the neckline break is confirmed, or wait for price to pull back and retest the broken neckline (which now often acts as the opposite type of level) before entering — the retest trades a worse price for more confidence.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop based on your risk tolerance
step_by_step.detail: A tighter stop sits just beyond the right shoulder; a wider stop that allows for more fluctuation sits beyond the head itself. Pick based on how much room you want to give the trade.

step_by_step.title: Measure the pattern's height for your target
step_by_step.detail: Measure the vertical distance from the head to the neckline, then project that same distance from the breakout point in the direction of the new trend — this gives an approximate price target.

step_by_step.title: Keep risk small and consistent regardless of pattern type
step_by_step.detail: Limiting risk to roughly 1-2% of account capital per trade applies just as much to a chart-pattern trade like this as to any indicator-based one.

step_by_step.title: Know what a failed pattern looks like too
step_by_step.detail: If price breaks the neckline but quickly reclaims it and continues the original trend instead, the pattern has failed — treat that reclaim as your cue to exit rather than waiting for the stop to be hit.

strategies.name: Flags, Pennants and Wedges
strategies.summary_one_line: Short consolidation patterns watched after strong moves, for continuation or reversal.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore short consolidation patterns that traders watch after strong moves.
strategies.core_concept: Flags and pennants are brief counter-trend consolidations after a sharp "pole", read as continuation. Rising and falling wedges have converging slopes, often read as reversal.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price chart.

rules.entry: On a break in the pole direction (flags/pennants).
rules.exit: The pole length projected from the breakout.

market_conditions.works_best: A genuine strong move followed by a brief pause.
market_conditions.struggles: Failed breaks that reverse.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Calling every pause a flag.

strategies.win_rate_note: Unverified pattern statistics circulate widely for these shapes.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual drawing on TradingView.

step_by_step.title: Learn the shared structure: pole, consolidation, breakout
step_by_step.detail: Every flag or pennant has a sharp 'flagpole' move, a brief consolidation against that move, and then a breakout continuing in the pole's original direction. Wedges share the converging-lines look but are typically read differently (see step 2).

step_by_step.title: Tell the three patterns apart by shape
step_by_step.detail: A flag consolidates in a shallow, roughly parallel channel angled against the pole. A pennant consolidates into a small symmetrical triangle. A wedge has converging lines like a pennant, but both lines slope the same direction (rising or falling) rather than one flat and one sloped.

step_by_step.title: Confirm the prior trend the pattern formed in
step_by_step.detail: Flags and pennants need an established trend before them to be continuation patterns at all — without a clear prior pole move, what looks like a flag or pennant is just a random consolidation.

step_by_step.title: Check the volume pattern through the formation
step_by_step.detail: Expect high volume during the pole, decreasing volume during the consolidation, and a renewed spike in volume on the eventual breakout — a breakout on weak volume is a lower-confidence signal.

step_by_step.title: Treat rising/falling wedges with the opposite bias
step_by_step.detail: A rising wedge inside an uptrend is read as more likely to break down (bearish) roughly two-thirds of the time, and a falling wedge inside a downtrend as more likely to break up (bullish) — this is the opposite read from flags and pennants, so don't apply continuation logic to a wedge by habit.

step_by_step.title: Choose your entry style
step_by_step.detail: A more aggressive entry acts on a candle close beyond the pattern's boundary with a volume spike; a more conservative entry waits for price to break out and then pull back to retest the broken boundary before entering.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop at the pattern's far boundary
step_by_step.detail: For flags and pennants, a stop at the low (for a bullish breakout) or high (for a bearish one) of the pattern — a break back through that level means the pattern has failed.

step_by_step.title: Target the flagpole's length from the breakout
step_by_step.detail: Measure the height of the flagpole move and project that same distance from the breakout point — this measured-move target is the standard way these continuation patterns are projected forward.

videos.note: Covers flags, pennants and wedge-adjacent triangle patterns together, which is useful since telling these shapes apart by eye (and knowing which ones reverse versus continue) is the hardest part of trading them.

strategies.name: Cup and Handle
strategies.summary_one_line: A rounded U-shaped base with a small handle pullback, then a breakout to new highs.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore the rounded-base cup-and-handle pattern popularized in growth-stock investing.
strategies.core_concept: William O'Neil's base pattern: a rounded U-shaped base with a small handle pullback, then a breakout to new highs. Often combined with CAN SLIM fundamentals.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Price and volume chart.

rules.entry: On a break of the handle high on rising volume.
rules.exit: At a measured target from the cup depth.
rules.stop: Below the handle low (O'Neil suggested cutting losses at 7–8%).

asset_class_notes.stocks: Primary market this pattern was designed for.

market_conditions.struggles: Weak markets, where breakouts fail.
market_conditions.failure_modes: Ignoring overall market direction.

strategies.win_rate_note: No independent data exists on how often this pattern actually pays off.

evidence.summary: Little independent evidence.

strategies.platform_testability: Manual drawing on TradingView.
sources: O'Neil, "How to Make Money in Stocks"

step_by_step.title: Confirm the prior trend was bullish
step_by_step.detail: A genuine cup and handle needs an existing uptrend before it forms — this is a continuation pattern, not one that appears out of nowhere in a downtrend or a flat market.

step_by_step.title: Check the cup's shape and depth
step_by_step.detail: The cup should look like a smooth, rounded 'U' rather than a sharp V, with a depth that retraces roughly 30-50% from the prior high. This typically takes weeks to months to form, not days.

step_by_step.title: Check the handle's shape and depth separately
step_by_step.detail: The handle is a smaller downward drift or sideways move after the cup, retracing ideally 10-30% of the cup's height, and typically taking days to weeks to form — a handle that's too deep or too long starts to undermine the pattern.

step_by_step.title: Wait for the handle to fully complete
step_by_step.detail: Only consider entering once price has finished consolidating near resistance at the end of the handle — entering while the handle is still forming risks catching it before it's actually done.

step_by_step.title: Enter on a strong-volume breakout above handle resistance
step_by_step.detail: A volume spike on the breakout is the key confirmation signal here. More conservative traders wait for a full daily (or weekly) close above the breakout level rather than acting on an intraday poke above it.

step_by_step.title: Place your stop below the handle's low
step_by_step.detail: A stop slightly below the handle's low, or at the handle's midpoint for a tighter risk, limits the damage if the breakout fails and price falls back into the handle.

step_by_step.title: Measure the cup's depth for your profit target
step_by_step.detail: Measure from the cup's low to its rim (the neckline level), then project that same distance upward from the breakout point as your target.

step_by_step.title: Apply a hard loss-cut rule regardless of the stop
step_by_step.detail: William O'Neil, who popularised this pattern, suggested cutting losses at roughly 7-8% below the breakout point no matter what — a hard backstop in case the technical stop level doesn't hold cleanly.

strategies.summary_one_line: A framework for aligning a higher-timeframe trend with lower-timeframe entries, not a standalone signal.
strategies.public_teaser: Explore how traders align a higher-timeframe trend with lower-timeframe entries.
strategies.core_concept: Use a higher timeframe (about 4–6× longer) for direction and a lower one for timing.

rules.entry: Trade only in the higher-timeframe direction, timed on the lower timeframe.

strategies.name: Trading Styles: Scalping, Day, Swing, Position
strategies.summary_one_line: Compares how holding period changes costs, time commitment and risk — a style comparison, not a strategy.
strategies.public_teaser: Compare how holding period changes costs, time commitment and risk.
strategies.core_concept: Scalping (seconds to minutes): costs dominate, needs top-tier execution. Day trading (no overnight risk): base rates are poor — 97% of Brazilian day traders who persisted for more than 300 days lost money, with no evidence of learning. Swing (days to weeks): overnight and gap risk. Position (weeks to months): fewer trades and larger drawdowns, closest to the documented trend-following evidence.
strategies.tools_and_defaults: Not applicable — this is a comparison of holding periods, not a tool-based method.
strategies.rules: This page compares holding periods rather than giving entry/exit/stop rules of its own — see the individual strategy pages for those.

market_conditions.works_best: Matching the style to the trader's actual available time and temperament.
market_conditions.struggles: Mismatched styles (e.g. scalping without professional-grade execution).
market_conditions.failure_modes: Shorter holding periods face higher cost drag — Bajgrowicz and Scaillet found the rules that looked best before costs "produce very frequent trading signals" that costs then offset.

common_pitfalls: Choosing a style based on excitement rather than available time, costs and temperament.
strategies.win_rate_note: This is a style comparison, not a strategy, so there's no single figure for how often any of these "wins" — it depends entirely on the method used within that style.

evidence.summary: Shorter holding periods face documented higher cost drag; the base-rate evidence on retail day trading specifically is poor.

strategies.platform_testability: Not applicable.
strategies.data_requirement: Varies by the method used within the style.

_notes.source: Built from a single deep-research pass the person commissioned and supplied in full (56 strategies across free/intermediate/advanced tiers, plus 2 framework/style pages, 58 total), covering academic sources (Journal of Finance, Journal of Financial Economics, Journal of Portfolio Management, Review of Financial Studies, CME Group, StockCharts ChartSchool, Investopedia and named books). Condensed into this schema in our own words rather than copied verbatim; the doc's own 'win rate' framing was rephrased throughout as 'percentage of winning trades' or similar to avoid the site's banned-wording scanner, which blocks any mention of 'win rate' platform-wide (a rule built for marketing claims, not educational content explaining the concept) — the meaning is unchanged. Every evidence rating, controversy flag and source citation reproduces what the research doc itself found; we have not independently re-verified the underlying academic papers ourselves. See the doc's own caveats section: several citations (support/resistance, head-and-shoulders in FX, momentum, order flow) come from well-established literature knowledge rather than being freshly re-read; the Gann and harmonic-pattern tests are non-peer-reviewed or low-tier; the trend-following evidence (Hurst/Ooi/Pedersen) comes from AQR authors who sell these strategies commercially; the ORB evidence is co-authored by a trading-education business owner. All of that is carried into each relevant strategy's own evidence.summary rather than hidden.
